title: Reflections on the Revolution in France
alternative_titles: Reflections on the French Revolution
description: The most powerful and most quoted attack on the French Revolution, thrown out as a long private letter made public within weeks of its writing. It refuses to try any constitution by the abstract rights of man, and pleads instead for prescription, for the inherited liberties of England, and for the moral institutions through which a nation ages gracefully. Its lament for the queen of France and its prophecy of a military adventurer sitting in judgment upon a nation made the book the founding text of modern conservative thought.
plot_or_argument: The argument opens by declining to congratulate the French on their new constitution, on the ground that the gift of abstract liberty to an unprepared people is a curse rather than a benefit. Against the rights of man it sets the rights of Englishmen, derived from an immemorial and prescriptive inheritance rather than from speculation, and it reads the Revolution of 1688 as a settlement of ancient law, not as the assertion of primitive freedom. Church, nobility, chivalry, and the landed interest are defended as the pillars that temper power and make subordination amiable; the confiscation of Church lands and the reduction of the clergy to a stipend are attacked as robbery dressed as reform. Where the abstractions triumph, the book predicts, the age of chivalry is gone, its successors a race of sophisters, economists, and calculators, and a degenerate democracy ends in the domination of an armed leader. The conclusion is an appeal to prejudice as a reasonable and social being, to the habitual sentiments that make a people warm to what the understanding alone could never make binding.
narrative_structure: A single sustained epistolary argument in no numbered divisions, rising from constitutional reasoning to prophecy, invective, and elegy; the set pieces on the queen of France and on the 'little platoons' of local attachment are structural climaxes rather than ornaments.
literary_form: political pamphlet in the form of a letter; polemic with historical and constitutional argument
meter_and_prosody: Large periodic prose of the parliamentary and pulpit schools, Latinate balance, apostrophe, and indignant interrogation, with a sustained rhetorical range from dry legal analysis to elegiac lament.
historical_context: Written in the spring and summer of 1790 in answer to a young correspondent's request for the author's sentiments, it broke with the Whig party and with the Society for Constitutional Information, and provoked an immediate swarm of replies, of which the most famous was the vindication of the rights of man published the next year. The celebration of the anniversary of the Bastille by a London dissenting congregation, whose sermon argued the right of a people to choose and to expel its rulers, supplied the occasion and the target of the whole book.
literary_significance: It established the vocabulary and the stock arguments of counter-Revolutionary thought, and it is the source of the enduring ideas of prescriptive liberty, of society as a partnership between the living, the dead, and the unborn, and of the claim that a state built on abstract political geometry dissolves the local attachments through which liberty is actually felt. Its influence runs through nineteenth-century conservatism and through the romantic dislike of abstraction; its critics, from the vindicators of natural rights to the pamphleteers of the 1790s, framed the whole British debate over Revolution.
attribution_notes: Attribution uncontested; the text is securely documented among the undisputed writings of its author, and its manuscript and printing history is well attested by contemporary correspondence and by the publisher's records.
bibliographical_notes: First published London, 1790, in quarto; it reached a second edition within a fortnight and several issues and translations within the year, and it was quickly reprinted in the American states. Modern scholarly editions annotate it against the author's parliamentary and correspondence papers.

title: An Appeal from the New to the Old Whigs
alternative_titles: Appeal from the New to the Old Whigs
description: A party pamphlet written as the author's Whig colleagues adopted the French Revolution as a principle, and addressed to the older Whig tradition of the Revolution of 1688 as he understood it. Its quarrel is less with France than with the leaders at home, and its method is quotation: it accumulates the language of the party's own classics to show that the new doctrines of popular sovereignty contradict the settled faith of the old.
plot_or_argument: The Appeal insists that the Revolution of 1688 was made to preserve the ancient law of the kingdom, not to create a right in any generation to model its government anew, and that the declaratory parts of the settlement bound Posterity as well as the present age. Against the position that the people at any moment may alter everything that offends them, it cites the party's own writers and the great common-law authorities, and it argues that an unlimited right of innovation is in fact a denial of all settled constitution. The book then examines the character of the new Whiggism, which it takes to have substituted metaphysical speculation for historical prescription, and it pleads that a party which abandons its own recorded principles forfeits its title to the name. Its closing judgement is that the true Old Whig is the man who holds the constitution as an inheritance to be transmitted unchanged.
narrative_structure: A continuous argument in long paragraphs, organized as an induction of witnesses: authorities and declared party opinions are quoted in sequence, then applied to the modern profession of faith.
literary_form: political pamphlet and party argument; polemic in the form of an appeal to authorities
meter_and_prosody: Forensic, cumulative prose, heavy with quotation and with the mannered courtesy of parliamentary invective; its characteristic movement is the citation followed by the dry comment.
historical_context: It followed the summer of 1791, when the leading figure of the parliamentary Whigs openly approved the French Revolution and when a meeting of the party's friends declared for the rights of men, driving the older, more constitutional Whigs into a separate allegiance. It arrived between the Reflections and the vindication of the rights of man, and it was read as the pamphlet that completed the rupture of the Whig interest.
literary_significance: It is the classic statement of prescriptive, party-based constitutionalism, and one of the earliest analyses of how a political language changes when a party adopts philosophy in place of history. Its method of appealing to an older canon of authorities became a permanent move in British conservative argument, and its account of the Revolution of 1688 was quoted for a century by both sides of the debate.
attribution_notes: Attribution uncontested as to the authorship of the argument; the manuscript was revised and corrected by a colleague in the Whig opposition whose share the author himself acknowledged in correspondence, a fact long recorded in the standard editions.
bibliographical_notes: First published London, 1791; it reached several issues within the year and was reprinted with the Reflections and the later letters in the collected editions of the author's works.

title: A Letter to a Member of the National Assembly
alternative_titles: Letter to a Member of the National Assembly
description: A short open letter published as a pendant to the constitutional polemic of the two previous years, answering a French correspondent who pressed the claim that the Revolution had given France a right to dictate the terms of opinion to its neighbours. It is compressed and angry, and it states the case against revolutionary propaganda in Europe more plainly than the longer book of 1790.
plot_or_argument: The letter grants that a people may reform its own government, but denies that any nation has a right to oblige its neighbours to accept a change of constitution as a model, and it treats the doctrine of a crusading Revolution as a menace to the settled order of Europe. It argues that the French assemblies have substituted the will of the moment for law, and that a government resting on such a basis must depend ultimately on force. Its most memorable claim is that a system founded on the destruction of all ancient institutions can end only in military rule, because nothing else remains to hold it together. The letter closes on the prospect of a Europe armed against a gospel of untried rights.
narrative_structure: A single unbroken epistolary argument, opening with the correspondent's plea, passing through the denial of the right of propagation, and ending in prophecy.
literary_form: open letter and political pamphlet; short polemical epistle
meter_and_prosody: Tight, satirical epistolary prose, more sententious and less ornamental than the Reflections, with the abrupt courtesy of a debater dismissing an opponent's premise.
historical_context: It appeared after the festival and oath of the Federation, when the French constitution seemed temporarily settled and when British societies of the friends of Revolution were urging address and imitation, and the author's alarm had turned from domestic party quarrel to the foreign policy of a propagandist state. It was written in the months before the declaration of war by France in the following spring.
literary_significance: It supplies the earliest clear statement of the argument against revolutionary war and against the international propagation of constitutional change by doctrine, later to be argued at length in the letters on a regicide peace. Its diagnosis of a Revolution that must become expansionist or militarise at home became a stock of nineteenth-century commentary on the Revolutionary settlement.
attribution_notes: Attribution uncontested; the letter is securely documented among the undisputed writings of its author and its correspondence occasion is recorded by the author himself.
bibliographical_notes: First published London, 1791, as a separate tract, and reprinted with the constitutional writings in the collected editions.

title: Letters on a Regicide Peace
alternative_titles: First Letter on a Regicide Peace
Letters on a Regicide Peace, and on the Prospects of a Regicide Success
description: Four open letters, the first two appearing in the autumn of 1795 and the remaining two in 1797, arguing against any negotiation with the French Directory. Their title is the argument: a state founded on the judicial murder of its king is a criminal association rather than a government, and to treat with it is to license regicide among the nations.
plot_or_argument: The first letter urges that the French power is not a France but a sect, organised for the destruction of all established government, so that peace with it would be a surrender disguised as moderation. The second argues at length that the apparent resources of the enemy are real and growing, and that the financial and military strength of the Republic has been systematically underrated by its British admirers. The third and fourth letters turn on the consequences of a pacification, prophesying the loss of the colonial and naval contest and the infection of the British constitution by a doctrine of untrimmed rights; the fourth, the most rhetorical, calls the Directory a military aggression in the shape of a civil government. Throughout, the letters press for the war as a war of principle rather than of balance, and for the internal restraint of the corresponding societies at home.
narrative_structure: Four letters of very unequal length forming a single sustained argument; the first two carry the case against negotiation, the third supplies the historical and philosophical defence of European society, the fourth is the closing peroration on the terms of a possible peace.
literary_form: political pamphlet in the form of open letters; war polemic and state-paper argument
meter_and_prosody: Amplified, declamatory prose of the late parliamentary style: long periods charged with metaphor, classical allusion, and invective, with an invectory rhythm the reviewers of the day imitated and mocked.
historical_context: Written during the debate on the negotiations at the close of 1795 and the talk of a congress in 1796-97, when the corresponding societies, the famine and the suspension of habeas corpus made the French question a domestic one. The letters were circulated as separate publications bought widely, and they fixed the language of the war party for a generation.
literary_significance: They carry the argument of the Reflections from constitutional theory into the diplomacy of ideological war, and they gave British political writing its most influential vocabulary for describing revolutionary power as a sect rather than a state. Their reading of the trade, finance and manpower of the enemy also marks an early attempt to argue grand strategy from social statistics.
attribution_notes: Attribution uncontested; the four letters are securely documented among the undisputed writings of their author, and their separate publication is well attested.
bibliographical_notes: First two letters published London, 1795; the third and fourth followed in 1797, and the four were collected at once in reprints and in the author's Works.

title: A Letter to a Noble Lord
alternative_titles: Letter to a Noble Lord
description: A vindication of himself and of the reward he had received from the Crown, written in answer to a peer's attack on pensions in a debate on the civil list. It is at once a personal apology, a history of the author's public services, and one of the great invectives against the new wealth of the war and against the aristocracy that flattered it.
plot_or_argument: The letter first pleads the modesty of a bounty granted for long service, and argues that a public reward conferred on a man who had served without profit is a praise of public spirit rather than a job. It then turns on the nobility, whose ancient wealth and station, it urges, were planted by wise statesmen and nursed by good princes for the shade of the commonwealth, and which now, having married its land to its ruin, sits in judgment on a single pension while it applauds the vast fortunes of the war. The anatomy of the new moneyed interest, with its influence upon the funds and its dependence upon the minister of the day, is the most quoted part of the book. The letter closes on the writer's own approaching death and on his refusal to be made an example by a party that wanted a precedent.
narrative_structure: A single long letter in three movements: personal vindication, historical and constitutional digression on the great oaks of the aristocracy, and the invective against paper fortune; the personal frame returns at the end.
literary_form: open letter and personal vindication; political invective with historical digression
meter_and_prosody: Sustained, indignant periodic prose, rich in metaphor of growth and decay, of trees and blight; the style of the late ornamental parliamentary manner at its fullest stretch.
historical_context: It was provoked by a debate in the House of Lords early in 1796, in which a duke moved for a committee on civil-list expenditure and attacked the pensions granted at the close of the American war, and by the attacks of a pamphleteer retained against the author. The book belongs to the scarcity and war-finance politics of 1796, when the fortunes made upon the funds had become a subject of moral argument.
literary_significance: It is the classic statement of the older critique of a moneyed interest by a servant of the landed constitution, and its passage on the 'great oaks' became the most quoted image of organic conservatism. As apology it is also the most autobiographical of the political writings, and it is the source most often read for the author's sense of service, poverty, and ingratitude.
attribution_notes: Attribution uncontested; the letter is securely documented among the undisputed writings of its author, though it is the most occasional and personal of them.
bibliographical_notes: First published London, 1796, as a separate quarto; several issues appeared within the year and the text was collected in the Works.

title: Rights of Man
alternative_titles: Rights of Man, Part the First and Part the Second
description: The great popular vindication of the French Revolution and of the rights of man, published in two parts, the first as an immediate answer to the counter-Revolutionary Reflections, the second as a systematic theory of government, a constitution for England, and a plan for public provision. It is the most widely read political book of the 1790s and the text that made its author a prosecution target in both countries.
plot_or_argument: Part the first denies that one generation can bind another, holds that a nation has a right to model its constitution at pleasure, and treats the American settlements as proof that society can be rebuilt upon the rights of man; the ancient-constitutional pleading of the Reflections is met with ridicule and with the claim that the Revolution of 1688 was no such inheritance. Part the second sets out first principles: civil government is a delegate of natural rights, none of which are surrendered, and every institution that does not add to the aggregate happiness of the community is an usurpation. It then analyses hereditary government as a civil species of despotism, and proposes annual national parliaments, manhood suffrage on a modest franchise, the abolition of place and monopoly, and a scale of taxation that falls on property in proportion to its excess. The celebrated closing plan is a system of public allowances for every person at every age of life, for education, for the old, and for the young, to be paid by a graduated contribution and by the abolition of aristocratic perquisites, and the book ends with the argument that a government of this kind is a condition of peace among nations as well as of happiness at home.
narrative_structure: Two parts of very different scale: the first a brisk occasional reply, the second a systematic treatise of principles, of constitutions, of finance and of social provision in numbered chapters.
literary_form: political pamphlet and treatise; polemic, constitutional scheme, and project of social provision
meter_and_prosody: Plain, direct, conversational prose addressed to the working reader, with sarcastic simplification of an opponent's argument, blunt arithmetic, and an evangelistic optimism of the new era.
historical_context: Part the first appeared within weeks of the constitutional polemic it answered and was suppressed within months; part the second, published early in 1792, was followed by a prosecution for seditious writing, by the author's flight and outlawry, and by the arrests of the societies that circulated it. The book supplied the creed of the British radical societies and of the Corresponding Society, and it was answered by a literature of loyalist pamphlets.
literary_significance: It is the founding text of popular radicalism in the English-speaking world and the strongest statement of natural-rights democracy between the American founding and the reform movement of the next century. Its second part, with its calculation that government is a national establishment for civil purposes and that the poor are creditors rather than objects of charity, shaped the language of welfare argument for a hundred years, and its style became the model of demotic political prose.
attribution_notes: Attribution to the author of the political writings is secure, but the share taken by one philosophic friend of the author's Paris period in the composition of the first part is a standing question in the biography of the text; the second part is undivided.
bibliographical_notes: Part the first published London, 1791, as a quarto; part the second published London, 1792, with a postscript containing a plan of a national constitution and a declaration of rights. Both parts were reprinted, pirated, and translated immediately, and the second ran through very large cheap issues. Standard scholarly text is the edition in the collected works of the author.

title: The Age of Reason
alternative_titles: The Age of Reason Part the First and Part the Second
description: The most widely circulated deist manifesto of the revolutionary decade, written in parts and published while its author was a prisoner in revolutionary France. Its first part states a creed of rational theism, denounces priestcraft as the corrupter of religion, and rejects the Bible as a collection of human and often obscene writings; the second part pursues the same argument through the Old Testament in detail. It made the case for unbelief in the plain, popular style of the pamphlet trade, and it was prosecuted, pirated, and answered by the whole religious press of two countries.
plot_or_argument: The book opens by professing belief in one God and by refusing the creed of any church, holding the study of the universe through its works to be the only true theology. From this it argues that the religion of revelation rests on hearsay, since no living generation can verify a miracle it has not itself seen, and that the evidence demanded for scripture is of a kind no court of law would receive. It then reads the biblical history as a record of cruelty, obscenity, and imposture, denies the divine origin of the book of Genesis and of the Mosaic law, and treats prophecy as an argument manufactured after the event. The church-and-state polemic follows: revealed religion, once made an establishment, becomes an engine of revenue and of persecution, and the moral character of the deity is impugned by the scriptures that pretend to reveal it. The closing position is the deist alternative: a universal, unclerical religion of creation, of benevolence, and of the rights of conscience, with the duties of man toward his neighbour as the whole of practical religion.
narrative_structure: Two parts of unequal argument: the first a statement of rational theism and of the evidential objection to revelation, the second a running critical examination of the Old Testament writings, each subdivided into short numbered chapters for cheap circulation.
literary_form: religious polemic and deist treatise; argumentative pamphlet with scriptural criticism
meter_and_prosody: Plain, contemptuous, colloquial argumentative prose, short sentences, direct address, and the demotic irony of the debating society; the rhetoric of evidence and common sense rather than of learning.
historical_context: Part the first was composed during the author's imprisonment in France and issued in the year of his release, in French translation and in London simultaneously; it was prosecuted in England, and the second part, appearing two years later, was answered by a stream of episcopal and evangelical replies. The book belongs to the radical religious culture of the 1790s, where the criticism of scripture followed naturally from the criticism of throne and altar.
literary_significance: It is the textbook of English popular deism and the most durable attack on scriptural authority between the deist controversy of the early eighteenth century and the rationalist theology of the nineteenth; it fixed for radicals the claim that a revealed religion cannot be evidenced, and for its opponents the problem of how to answer a lay reader without scholarship. Its frankness, and the biography of its composition in a prison, made its author a martyr figure for freethought, and its arguments reappear in the sceptical literature of the following century.
attribution_notes: Attribution uncontested; a projected further part survives in manuscript and in report, and the editions of the early nineteenth century differ in the material they admit, so the volume of any given issue is not a reliable guide to what its author sanctioned.
bibliographical_notes: Part the first published in 1794, in Paris in French translation and in London in English; part the second published in 1796; parts were reprinted, prosecuted, and pirated repeatedly, and later collected editions gathered the surviving manuscripts. The first London issue is often found with the emblematic frontispiece of the later editions.

title: Agrarian Justice
alternative_titles: Agrarian Justice Opposed to the Agrarian Law
description: A short pamphlet of political economy and justice, addressed to the problem of property in land and proposing a national fund paid from landed and inheritable wealth. It distinguishes the earth in its natural state, the common inheritance of all, from the earth in a state of cultivation, whose improvements are property, and argues that the landholder owes a rent to the community for the ground he holds. Its practical proposal, an endowment paid to every citizen at majority and a pension in old age, is the most quoted part of the work.
plot_or_argument: The pamphlet begins by rejecting both the levelers and the defenders of prescription: agrarian laws confounding property with the land are unjust, but the exclusive private ownership of the earth by inheritance is a theft of the common stock. It then dates the revolution of property: cultivation created the value of land, and with it the inequality that dispossessed the many for the benefit of the few, so that civilization, instead of diminishing, has increased the mass of misery. From this it concludes that the occupant of land owes a ground-rent to the national estate, but that the improvements belong to the holder and are not to be confiscated. The scheme follows: a national fund raised by a duty upon inheritances beyond the direct line, and administered as a payment to every person reaching adulthood and as an annuity for those advanced in years, with the poor laws to be repealed as inefficient and degrading. The argument closes by claiming that this plan relieves the poor without pauperising them, and enriches no one at the expense of the donor.
narrative_structure: A continuous short argument in nine numbered sections: the statement of the common right, the history of cultivated property, the refutation of confiscation, the ground-rent principle, the plan of the national fund, and the objections answered.
literary_form: pamphlet in political economy and social project; argumentative tract with a scheme of public provision
meter_and_prosody: Ardent, arithmetical prose of the plain school: declaratory openings, numbered cases, and a repeated rhythm of 'it is not, but it is' distinctions, pitched for the popular reader.
historical_context: Written in France during the Directory, in the aftermath of the constitutional pamphlets of the same years and of the debate over agrarian law in the American states, and published in 1797 in Paris, Philadelphia, and London. Its appearance coincided with the British controversy over the poor laws, of which the tract's argument was a radical version.
literary_significance: It is the classical statement of the doctrine that landed property is a social creation carrying a debt to the community, the source of the long tradition that connects the unearned increment to public endowment, and one ancestor of both the single-tax tradition and the modern case for a social dividend. Its tone also made it a permanent weapon in the argument over property, quoted alike by radicals and by their opponents.
attribution_notes: Attribution uncontested; the work is securely documented among the undisputed writings of its author, and its dedication to the French Directory is printed in the first issue.
bibliographical_notes: First published 1797, at Paris, with contemporary issues at Philadelphia and London; reprinted repeatedly in the cheap radical press of the nineteenth century and collected in the author's works.

title: Dissertation on First Principles of Government
alternative_titles: Dissertation on the First Principles of Government
description: A compressed summary of the author's political philosophy, first printed in an American newspaper and soon reissued as a tract in Britain, arguing that the rights of man are the only foundation of a lawful constitution and that hereditary government is a usurpation over the living. It is the plainest and most catechetical of the revolutionary writings, and it was used for a century as a schoolbook of democracy.
plot_or_argument: The dissertation states first that the only moral bond of society is the interest of the living, and that no generation has authority over another; from this it follows that a nation has a right to frame and to alter its constitution at its will, and that the constitutions of men may be as various as the circumstances of men. It then distinguishes the rights of man from the powers of government, holds that all power improperly delegated is the origin of abuse, and treats hereditary succession as a fraud against the consent of the governed and a source of war. Representation is advanced as the true and simple device by which a nation acts, in place of the person of a king, and the argument ends with the claim that a government of this kind must be pacific at home and confederate abroad, so that the rights of nations and the rights of men are one system.
narrative_structure: A short dissertation in continuous sections without numbered chapters, moving from first principles to the criticism of hereditary government, then to representation, and closing on the prospect of a pacific system of nations.
literary_form: political treatise in pamphlet form; first-principles argument and constitution theory
meter_and_prosody: Aphoristic, declaratory prose, largely free of ornament and built out of reiterated definitions; the manner of the public lecture and of the catechism.
historical_context: Published in the year of the author's release from imprisonment and of the controversy over the constitution of the French Republic, and printed first in Philadelphia and then as a separate tract in London, where it entered the circulating libraries with the rest of the revolutionary literature. It was prosecuted in England along with the earlier political writings.
literary_significance: It distils the natural-rights case into its shortest and most quotable form, and it supplied the vocabulary of nineteenth-century democratic and republican movements in both hemispheres. Its insistence that constitutions are ordinary social devices rather than inheritances is the plainest statement of the doctrine the romantic critics of abstraction were later to attack from the other side.
attribution_notes: Attribution uncontested; the text is securely documented among the undisputed writings of its author, and its first newspaper publication and subsequent separate issues are recorded in the contemporary accounts.
bibliographical_notes: First printed in a Philadelphia newspaper in 1795, and published as a separate tract in London in the same year with the author's name; frequently reprinted alone and in the collected works.

title: An Enquiry Concerning Political Justice
alternative_titles: Enquiry Concerning Political Justice
Political Justice
description: The most ambitious attempt of the revolutionary decade to found a system of politics, morals, and the human mind upon the single principle of private judgement. Written in three volumes by a dissenting minister who had abandoned his pulpit, it argues that government is an evil, that institutions corrupt the understanding, and that a rational society could dispense with punishment, property, and marriage. It fixed the creed of the radical philosophical circle and drew upon its author a lifetime of controversy.
plot_or_argument: The enquiry opens from the perfectibility of man: a rational creature, governed by opinion, is capable of indefinite improvement, and the mischief of the world proceeds from institutions that fix and pervert his judgement. Government it treats as a necessary evil at best, a force that substitutes the decision of one for the decision of the many and that rests on the very error it is meant to correct; it should therefore be reduced to the smallest possible extent, and its functions of punishment and of legislation dissolved into the verdict of unprejudiced understanding. On property the first edition argues that each has a claim upon the surplus of another's stock when his own wants are greater, that accumulation is the child of law and of opinion, and that a rational distribution would follow the general good. Marriage and the obligations of promise are examined as contracts which an independent judgement cannot be bound to keep; and the same argument is applied to oaths, to colonies, to wealth, to the theatre, to literature, and to population, each of which is shown to be a corruption of a simple moral truth. The closing books defend truth-telling as a duty absolute enough to outweigh the claim of a murderer, and treat political reform as a question of opinion, to be advanced by discussion and not by violence.
narrative_structure: Three volumes of essays in strict sequence: the principles of political morality and of the mind, the actual institutions of civil society criticized one by one, and the practical conduct of reform; each chapter a self-contained argument with a numbered heading.
literary_form: philosophical treatise of politics and morals; systematic enquiry in essays
meter_and_prosody: Austere, impersonal, relentlessly syllogistic prose: short paragraphs of premise and conclusion, the abstract noun as the subject of almost every sentence, and an absence of ornament that became itself a style.
historical_context: Published in the same months as the counter-revolutionary constitutional writings were provoking the vindication of the rights of man, and composed by a minister of the new philosophy of necessity who had already written a treatise on the same system of morals. It circulated as the creed-book of the radical societies and of the philosophical circle, and it provoked the most famous of all its replies, an essay on population written to disprove the perfectibility it assumed.
literary_significance: It is the founding text of philosophical anarchism and one of the two or three works that shaped the radical romantic imagination of the 1790s, converting the doctrine of private judgement into a complete social criticism. Its influence on the poets of the following generation, on the communitarian and freethought movements, and on the later debate over justice, property, and punishment, is one of the main lines of intellectual history of the period.
attribution_notes: Attribution uncontested; the text is not, however, a single stable work, since the author recast and retracted much in the second edition, and the editions differ enough that any claim about his doctrine of property and of promise must specify its year.
bibliographical_notes: First published London, 1793, in three volumes; a much altered second edition in 1798, with the doctrines of property, marriage, and promise softened, and a final edition with a preface and notes appearing in the third decade of the century. The modern scholarly edition prints the variants of the successive texts.

title: An Essay on the Principle of Population
alternative_titles: Essay on the Principle of Population
description: The tract that refused the perfectibility of the species a place in the rational political future, published anonymously and written to answer the philosophy of indefinite improvement then current among the radical writers of the day. Its principle is arithmetical and pitiless: population, if unchecked, doubles in a generation, while food cannot be made to increase beyond a far slower rate, and the surplus must therefore be taken off by vice, by misery, or by restraint. It is the founding document of population science and of the political economy of the poor.
plot_or_argument: The essay lays down two postulates in the constitution of man, the passion between the sexes and the need of food, and a third proportion, that population in a country without checks goes on doubling every five-and-twenty years while the produce of even improved agriculture advances only in an arithmetical series. From these it deduces that the race of man cannot be improved away from suffering, since every improvement of subsistence is consumed by the increased numbers it supports, and that equality and a community of goods would in a few years reproduce all the inequality they abolished. It then surveys the checks actual and possible: vice and misery, war, famine, disease, and late and unfruitful marriage as the only check consistent with virtue and with the happiness of the poor. The argument is applied to the parish provisions of England, which it holds to accelerate population without creating food and so to aggravate the evil they profess to cure, and to the laws of settlement, to interest, and to the practice of charitable accumulation of grain. In the second edition, recast on an enlarged scale, the historical and statistical evidence of the checks is worked out through the ages and nations of the world, with the American states as the proof of what a cheap land and prudent marriage can do, and with the moral check of delayed marriage advanced as the practical remedy.
narrative_structure: In the first issue a short sequence of numbered chapters stating the principle, its illustration, and its consequences for the systems of improvement; in the recast edition a much enlarged two-volume argument of statistical history, of the checks in the ancient and modern world, and of the applications to the law and the politics of the poor.
literary_form: treatise of political economy and social theory; statistical essay with polemic
meter_and_prosody: Cool, numerate, candid prose of the investigating mind: postulate, ratio, and consequence, with a candour of pessimism that became a rhetorical pose in itself.
historical_context: It grew out of a family discussion on the schemes of human perfectability and was published in the year after the war, the scarcity, and the agitation that followed the revolutionary decade, when the English controversy over the poor laws was opening. Its author, a fellow of a Cambridge college and the holder of the first English chair of political economy, wrote into the second edition the agricultural and statistical evidence of the following years, and the work went through successive editions to the middle of the century.
literary_significance: It is the origin of demography as a science and one of the two or three books that made the argument from necessity indispensable to social thought; it defeated the philosophy of perfectability on its own ground, supplied the naturalists of the next century with the premise of the struggle for existence, and set the terms in which poverty, marriage, relief, and empire were debated for a hundred years. Its tone, at once humane and unsparing, made it the most attacked book of the generation and the standard example of the 'dismal' science.
attribution_notes: Published anonymously, and the authorship was openly acknowledged by its author within a few years and in the later editions; the two very different forms of the first and second editions raise no question of attribution but do require the text to be cited by edition.
bibliographical_notes: First published London, 1798, in one octavo volume, anonymously, with a title referring to the speculations of two modern writers on the improvement of society; a second edition, greatly enlarged and restructured, appeared in 1803 in two volumes, with further editions by the author to the sixth. Standard scholarly text the facsimile of the first edition and the variorum edition of the subsequent texts.

title: A View of the Evidences of Christianity
alternative_titles: View of the Evidences of Christianity
description: The standard manual of natural and evidential theology of the decade, prepared over many years and published at the moment when the French scepticism seemed to threaten the establishment. It treats the Christian records as a case at law, examines the evidence of the apostles as witnesses, and argues that a candid reader, weighing testimony of the kind a court would receive, must believe. It went through many editions and was the prescribed reading of a generation of undergraduates.
plot_or_argument: The view first defines the nature of the evidence, which is not the internal evidence of a presumed inspiration but the external, circumstantial testimony of history, of the same sort upon which civil and criminal judgements are daily passed. It then examines the witnesses: the apostles and their contemporaries, whose belief in a resurrection they had not themselves seen, whose candour is proved by their frank recording of their own weakness and of the incredulity of their master's kindred, and whose suffering makes imposture impossible, since no knave endures what they endured for a story of his own making. The miracle evidence is treated as the strongest part of the case, because miracles were demanded as proof and were attested by persons who had the means and the motive to detect imposture. The undesigned coincidences of the several writers, agreeing without concert, are urged as evidence of authenticity, and the whole is closed by an answer to the objections from the number of competing religions, from the secrecy of the evidence, and from the slow diffusion of the faith.
narrative_structure: Two volumes in five parts: the nature and force of evidence in general, the evidence for the Christian history considered as a case of testimony, the miracle evidence, the objection and answer, and the practical conclusion urging the weight of the proof upon the candid mind.
literary_form: evidential and apologetical treatise; natural and revealed theology in the legal-proof manner
meter_and_prosody: Lucid, workmanlike, unhurried argumentative prose: the courtroom idiom of fact and witness, definition followed by example, and a diffused good humour that made severe reasoning easy reading.
historical_context: Composed slowly from the lectures and reading of the previous two decades and published in the year of the thanksgiving and of the debates over infidelity, when the deist and sceptical pamphlets of the revolutionary decade made an orderly defence of the evidence a party as well as a Church cause. It was read with the author's moral and political treatise as the textbook of the establishment's divinity.
literary_significance: It is the most influential English apology of the period, the classic example of the reduction of religion to a question of historical testimony, and the book by which the legal and evidential school of theology reached its plainest expression. Its treatment of undesigned coincidence passed into the equipment of every later apologist, and its assumption that faith is a verdict upon evidence became the position romantic and fideist writers of the following century set themselves to dispute.
attribution_notes: Attribution uncontested; the work is securely documented among the undisputed writings of its author, and the long gestation of the text is recorded in the biographical and correspondence material.
bibliographical_notes: First published London, 1794, in two volumes; numerous editions, American reprints, and abridgements for schools followed within the author's lifetime, and it remained a prescribed university text into the middle of the nineteenth century.

title: Horae Paulinae
alternative_titles: Horae Paulinae; or, New Confirmed Evidences of the Divine Authority of the Holy Scriptures
description: A critical-apologetical experiment, comparing the letters of the apostle Paul with the narrative of the Acts and with one another, and finding in their accidental agreements a proof of authenticity no forger could have produced. It is a work of scholarship used as evidence, and its method of undesigned coincidence became one of the most copied arguments in the defence of the scriptures.
plot_or_argument: The treatise first states its rule: if two writers, writing independently and for different purposes, touch upon the same place, person, or incident in ways neither intended nor adverted to, and yet without contradiction, their concurrence is evidence that both were dealing with real transactions. It then applies the rule, setting the letters of the Thessalonians and of the Corinthians beside the narrative of the missionary journeys, and showing that the history and the epistles supply each other's omissions, that the characters, fortunes, and fellow-labourers agree without apparent study, and that the notices of the collection for the poor saints at Jerusalem fall into place only when the two records are read together. A second line of comparison is drawn between the epistles themselves, whose differences of tone, of phrase, and of circumstance are shown to be marks of genuine correspondence rather than of a designed uniformity. The conclusion is that these writings are neither forged nor colluded, and that the same method may be extended to the rest of the canon.
narrative_structure: Parts, each pairing one epistle or group of epistles with the corresponding portion of the narrative, and closing with general remarks on the extent and force of the concurrence; the argument proceeds by accumulated particulars rather than by deduction.
literary_form: critical dissertation and biblical commentary in the evidential manner
meter_and_prosody: Quiet, patient, expository prose of the close reader: parallel text, minute comparison, and the restrained exultation of a reasoner who believes he has found a new class of proof.
historical_context: Published in the year of the counter-revolutionary pamphlets and of the quarrel over infidelity, out of the same school of evidential divinity that produced a popular view of the Christian proof, and built upon a method its author had already worked out in private study before the sceptical crisis made such arguments a public need.
literary_significance: It created a permanent instrument of scriptural apologetic, the argument from undesigned coincidence, which passed into commentaries, into the popular evidential manuals, and into the literary criticism of the next century, where the same test was used to date and to authenticate documents. As criticism it anticipates the modern treatment of a correspondence as historical evidence, and as rhetoric it is the neatest example of the period's habit of arguing religion from the rules of proof.
attribution_notes: Attribution uncontested; the work is securely documented among the undisputed writings of its author, who afterwards re-cast and enlarged portions of it in the collected editions of his theological works.
bibliographical_notes: First published London, 1790, in one volume; reissued with additions and in combination with the author's other evidential writings in several editions before and after his death.

title: Natural Theology
alternative_titles: Natural Theology; or, Evidences of the Existence and Attributes of the Deity
description: The classic statement of the argument from design, opening with the famous supposition of a watch found upon a heath and proceeding to argue that what the watch is to a watchmaker, the structure of animals and plants is to a Deity. It gathers the contrivances of the organic world, eye, joint, bone, leaf, instinct, and the mutual relations of species, into a single cumulative case, and it remains the plainest and most seductive English form of the natural theology of design.
plot_or_argument: The treatise begins by showing that a complex instrument found in a field forces the inference of an intelligence that made and placed it, and that the inference is not weakened by the ignorance of the finder as to its use. It then carries the analogy into the organic world: the jointed frame, the muscles, the circulation, the secretion, and above all the eye, with its lens, its humours, and its adaptation to distances, present the same relation of parts to a purpose which in any other case we refer to design. Following parts examine the contrivances of the sexes, of the provision for the young, of the structure of plants and seeds, of the instincts, of the relations of animals to their elements and to one another, and of the great balance by which the increase of each species is restrained. The closing argument turns from contrivance to the attributes, meets the difficulty of the suffering found in organic nature, and urges that the goodness as well as the power of the maker is to be collected from the preponderance of enjoyment in the system.
narrative_structure: A continuous treatise in numbered chapters without parts or volumes, rising from the single analogy of the instrument through the anatomy of contrivance to the inquiry after the attributes of the designer and the problem of organic suffering.
literary_form: natural theology; teleological treatise built on anatomical and natural-history evidence
meter_and_prosody: Plain, homely, convincingly orderly prose, with the concrete instance always at hand and the analogy pressed home by repetition; the manner of the excellent teacher who distrusts ornament.
historical_context: Published at the close of the century of natural history and of the anatomical schools, when the accumulated detail of the organic world offered itself as evidence, and when the sceptical handling of the design argument in the previous generation had made a restatement of it a duty of the pulpit; the author's own medical and anatomical reading, and the natural-history literature of the day, supply the whole texture of the book.
literary_significance: It is the received text of the argument from design in English, the book against which the later nineteenth century measured its own revolution in biology, and one of the most widely read and most quoted works of natural theology of any period. Its influence is also a literary influence: the analogy of the watch, and the habit of reasoning from contrivance, entered the common stock of the period's writing on nature and remain the standard form the teleological argument still takes in popular discussion.
attribution_notes: Attribution uncontested; the work is securely documented among the undisputed writings of its author, whose long delay in publishing it is recorded by his family and by his biographers.
bibliographical_notes: First published London, 1802, in one volume, with an edition paid for by a divinity library subscription; it reached a large number of editions and translations, American and British, through the century, and it was abridged for schools.

title: Natural Theology (Bridgewater Treatise)
description: The first of the treatises founded by a ducal bequest for the demonstration of the power, wisdom, and goodness of God in the creation, and the most ambitious restatement of the design argument of its generation. Its plan is to show that the inorganic world is fitted to man before man is fitted to it, and that no advance of physical explanation touches the inference from contrivance to a contriving intelligence.
plot_or_argument: The treatise distinguishes two branches of the argument, the physical, which inquires how things are done, and the metaphysical, which inquires why they are done and by whose choice; the one, it urges, can go for ever without ever superseding the other, because a law of nature names a regularity and never an agency. It then examines the properties of matter, the atmosphere, the relations of heat and light, the water cycle, and the constitution of the globe, and reads them as a series of anticipations of human need, so that the world appears prepared for its inhabitant before the inhabitant exists. From the inorganic it passes to the organic, to the structure of plants and animals, to the instincts, and to the mutual restraints by which the increase of every species is bounded. The closing argument collects the attributes: unity of counsel displayed in the mutual adjustment of separate contrivances, intelligence, power, and beneficence; and it meets the difficulties from animal suffering and from apparent waste by insisting upon the preponderance of enjoyment and upon the ignorance of the whole plan.
narrative_structure: Two volumes in numbered discourse-chapters: the distinction of the physical and metaphysical branches, the evidence from inorganic nature, the evidence from organic nature, and the collection of the attributes with the answer to the accompanying difficulties.
literary_form: natural theology; teleological treatise in the Bridgewater series
meter_and_prosody: Diffusive, animated, preacher-like prose of great range: cumulative enumeration, abrupt address to the sceptic, and a rhetorical exultation in the vastness of the evidence, held together by the distinction between how and why.
historical_context: Written for a series founded by the will of a noble testator and endowed for the express purpose of a nineteenth-century statement of creation's evidence, at a moment when the physical sciences were making their largest claims and when the evidence from geology and from anatomy had begun to disturb the older teleologies. Its author, at that time a Glasgow professor and the most powerful preacher of the evangelical party in the Church of Scotland, was chosen for the series on the strength of that reputation.
literary_significance: It is the last great English attempt to make the argument from design secure against mechanism by dividing the two inquiries into different questions, a move that has remained the standard theistic reply to scientific explanation; and its treatment of the fitness of the environment to life set the agenda for the later 'adaptation' theologies of the Victorian crisis of faith. As rhetoric it is the finest single performance of the popular theological style of its author, and it was read across the Atlantic as well as in Britain.
attribution_notes: Attribution uncontested; the treatise is securely documented among the undisputed writings of its author and holds its allotted place in the endowment series.
bibliographical_notes: First published 1823, as the first of a series of treatises founded by a bequest for the evidence of the creation; it reached several editions and translations, and it was abridged and reprinted within the series throughout the century.

title: The Christian and Civic Economy of Large Towns
alternative_titles: Christian and Civic Economy of Large Towns
description: A series of discourses on the moral government of great cities, written out of the practical work of a Glasgow parish and addressed to the failure of the centralized administration of religion and of relief in the masses. It argues that neither church nor poor-law can reach a population that has no local ties, and that the remedy is territorial: a resident pastorate, a district school, and a face-to-face administration of charity.
plot_or_argument: The discourses begin with the observation that the populous units of a great city are not a society but a multitude, without mutual knowledge, without local attachment, and without the relations in which character is formed; the institutions of the established church and the parish machinery of the poor-law, administered over so wide a field and by agents who never see the persons, therefore miss their mark and may even make matters worse. It then pleads for the division of the town into small districts, each with its own school, its own resident minister or visitor, and its own administration of relief, so that the eye of the governor and the eye of the governed may meet. The argument proceeds to the economy of charity, distinguishing the alms that pamper idleness from the provision that is earned, anticipated, and repaid in character, and it urges the voluntary principle and the cooperation of the subscribed district. It closes with the claim that this territorial religion is the only machinery that can carry Christianity to the mass at all, and that a city so organised would be at once more moral and more cheaply governed.
narrative_structure: Discourses I and following, published in parts and afterwards gathered into a volume, each part a single sustained argument from the observation of the city to the proposal of the district plan.
literary_form: practical and pastoral treatise on social administration; sermon-discourse with a plan of reform
meter_and_prosody: Vivid, urban, statistical prose of the popular pulpit: enumerated masses, the rhetorical question, the homely analogy, and a moral urgency that stops short of invective.
historical_context: Written while its author was translating into practice the district schemes he had tried in the poor parishes of a manufacturing city growing with unprecedented speed, and in the years when the town-planted church, the session of the district, and the debate over the poor laws were becoming the great questions of British social policy. The book belongs to the movement that made the moral condition of the towns a national subject.
literary_significance: It is the classic statement of the territorial cure for the city, and one of the most influential texts in the history of the district-visiting, the endowed district church and school, and the machinery that preceded the later municipal and welfare administration; its analysis of the multitude without local bonds anticipates a permanent theme of social writing. Its mixture of statistics, sermon, and administrative proposal also makes it a landmark of the new prose on the industrial town.
attribution_notes: Attribution uncontested; the discourses are securely documented among the undisputed writings of their author, and the practical work out of which they grew is recorded in his own accounts and correspondence.
bibliographical_notes: First published at Glasgow in parts from 1821, and gathered into volumes with the later discourses; several editions appeared within a few years, with English and American issues.

title: Strictures on the Modern System of Female Education
alternative_titles: Strictures on the Modern System of Female Education; in a Series of Letters
description: The most widely read conduct book of the decade, addressed to the education of girls and young women and written against the fashionable seminary system and against the theories of female independence then in circulation. Cast as a series of letters, it argues that accomplishments without principle, and learning without religion, produce not accomplished women but spoiled ones, and that the true end of female education is character.
plot_or_argument: The letters begin with the complaint that the new system has exchanged solidity for show, that the seminary teaches a little of everything and nothing thoroughly, and that the French Revolution, by loosing all authority, has corrupted female manners as it has corrupted public principle. It then examines the accomplishments in detail, music, drawing, French, and the small literature of the closet, and finds that they consume the time and destroy the simplicity which the domestic and religious duties require. Against the popular vindications of female rights it urges that the office of woman is not to contest her station but to fill it well, and that her influence, which is real and great, is lost when it is spent on display. The later letters set out the positive scheme: the formation of habit, the government of the temper, the cultivation of cheerful piety, the training for the trials of life, and the duty of the mother as the first educator; and the whole is closed by an appeal to the Christian standard as the only rule that will hold a woman in the day of temptation and of sorrow.
narrative_structure: A series of letters in two volumes, arranged by topics rather than by a narrative: the general charge against the modern system, the criticism of the accomplishments and of the fashionable reading, the vindication of the female office, and the positive scheme of habit, temper, and piety.
literary_form: conduct and educational treatise in epistolary form; familiar moral argument
meter_and_prosody: Brisk, pointed, indignant yet obliging prose, full of antithesis and of the shrewd particular illustration, with a woman writer's command of the domestic detail; the tone of persuasion sharpened by reproach.
historical_context: Published in the decade of the controversy over female education opened by the vindications of the rights of women, when the seminaries and the new female literature had become a public question, and when the fear of French principles made the government of the family a subject of national anxiety. Its author was already the most skilful manager of religious publishing in the country, and the book sold in large editions and was answered as well as praised.
literary_significance: It is the central document of the conservative reply to the women question in the 1790s, and the form in which the arguments from duty, character, and influence were put against the arguments from rights; it shaped the practice of the girls' schools and of the conduct literature of the following generation. As social description it preserves, more vividly than any treatise of the period, the actual accomplishments, reading, and expectations of the educated young woman of the rank it addressed.
attribution_notes: Attribution uncontested; the work is securely documented among the undisputed writings of its author, whose private and public educational work is recorded in the biographical literature.
bibliographical_notes: First published London, 1799, in two volumes, in the form of letters; it reached numerous editions and translations, and an American edition followed immediately.

title: The Cheap Repository Tracts
alternative_titles: The Cheap Repository
description: A series of small religious and moral tracts, sold at the halfpenny and the penny, launched to supply the labouring poor with wholesome reading in place of the chapbook, the penny song, and the political pamphlet. Written mostly by one hand with the help of a few contributors, and paid for by subscription, it is the first organised experiment in the mass religious circulation of cheap print in England.
plot_or_argument: The design is stated in the series' own terms: to imitate the form and the price of the corrupted chapbook while supplying it with Christian matter, so that the reader who would buy the obscene tale or the seditious song may buy instead a story that recommends industry, honesty, sobriety, and the church. The tracts therefore fall into an argument by example: the village tale of the good and bad servant, the dialogue of the ignorant labourer instructed by his superior, the account of a pious parish, and the plain exposition of the catechism and of the Sunday; each insists that religion is a practical rule of life and that the poor man's true comfort is his duty cheerfully done. Alongside the instruction runs a political argument in the same keys, the duty of submission to the established government, the danger of the new philosophy, and the blessing of the country's constitution. The series also carries a case for the religious education of the poor, and for the reading of the scripture in a form that may be trusted.
narrative_structure: A continuously issued series of small tracts, generally of a few pages, in prose dialogue, tale, and exposition, each complete in itself and numbered as it appeared; the units were afterwards gathered in collected series.
literary_form: religious and moral tract; didactic tale and dialogue for the labouring reader
meter_and_prosody: Deliberately plain, colloquial, and dramatic prose, with the homely proverb, the dialogue of the ignorant and the knowing, and a warm humour of the village; the style of the tract as a designed instrument of persuasion.
historical_context: Founded in the spring of 1795 in the heat of the counter-Revolutionary anxiety, when the circulation of cheap political and sceptical print among the labouring classes had become a subject of alarm to the government and to the religious societies, and supported by subscriptions from the nobility and the bishops. Its machinery of circulation, by which the tracts were sent out in astonishing numbers and dispersed through the country by the country subscribers, was the model of the tract society that followed.
literary_significance: It is the origin of the tract as an instrument of national religious and political circulation, the ancestor of the great tract societies of the nineteenth century, and an epoch in the history of reading among the poor, since it first proposed to reach the labouring reader on his own terms of price, form, and language. It also fixed a permanent stereotype of the didactic tale of the virtuous labourer, and it provoked the first great debate about the effect of cheap print upon the opinions of the people.
attribution_notes: The series is a joint undertaking in its circulation and in a few of its numbers, but the great majority of the tracts are from one hand; the individual numbers are variously dated and reattributed in the collected series, and the exact contents of any given collected issue vary.
bibliographical_notes: Issued in London from 1795 under the head of a 'Cheap Repository', at halfpenny, penny, and twopenny prices; the numbers were reprinted in collected series, many of them for the American market, and the whole ran into millions of copies within a few years.

title: Practical Piety
alternative_titles: Practical Piety; or, the Influence of the Power of Godliness on the Felicity of this Life and of Eternity
description: A long devotional and practical work addressed to persons of rank and fortune, urging that true religion is not a form but a power governing the actual hours and business of the world. It belongs to the author's later religious writings, in which the evangelic argument is turned from the poor to the rich, and happiness itself is pleaded as the reward of godliness.
plot_or_argument: The work distinguishes the form of godliness from its power, and charges the religious world of leisure with a piety of seasons and of duties rather than of the heart, a religion of the closet and the Sunday which leaves the closet and the week unaltered. It then examines the practical influence of genuine religion upon the felicity of this life: upon time, which the religious person redeems from trifling and from the tyranny of engagement; upon the temper, upon the affections, upon the use of wealth and of hospitality, and upon the society of the world, where it claims that a sober and obliging piety is more amiable and more successful than the manners it condemns. The later parts turn to the trials of life, sickness, loss, disappointment, and the death of those beloved, and argue that a religion which does not meet these has not been tried. The conclusion urges the eternal motive: that the same principle which makes the present life happy is the only security for the happiness of another.
narrative_structure: A continuous practical-divinity argument in books or volumes of headed chapters, each unit a distinct branch of the influence examined, with scriptural text and practical application throughout.
literary_form: practical divinity and devotional prose; religious conduct treatise
meter_and_prosody: Warm, persuasive, particularised prose of the experienced religious writer: direct address to the person of rank, the vivid little case from real life, the balanced period, and an unembarrassed use of the motive of happiness.
historical_context: Written in the author's later period, after the tract enterprise and the Mendip school labours had turned her argument from the religion of the poor to the responsibility of the rich, and in the season of the evangelical and dissenting controversy over experimental religion. Its appeal to the leisured classes of the metropolis and the county belonged to the same movement that produced the society and the charity-school literature of the war years.
literary_significance: It is one of the most widely circulated of the later practical-divinity books, and a key text of the religion of sensibility turned to use: its claim that piety and present happiness are the same thing was one of the strongest answers of the evangelical party to the charge that religion is ascetic and antisocial. Its portraiture of the religious world of fashion, in its mixture of counsel and satire, preserves the manners of its class with unusual exactness.
attribution_notes: Attribution uncontested; the work is securely documented among the undisputed writings of its author.
bibliographical_notes: First published London, 1811, in volumes; several editions and an American reprint followed within a few years, and it was afterwards gathered with the author's other religious works.

title: Chrestomathia
description: A plan of day-education for the middle and working classes, printed with a coined title word for the 'useful learning' it proposed, and one of the most original of the period's educational books. It sets out a curriculum of positive knowledge, an economical organisation of teaching, and a withering criticism of the monopoly of classical learning and of the boarding-school.
plot_or_argument: The treatise first defines the chrestomathic method as the instruction of youth in that portion of stock of ideas which is useful to the individual and to the community, and charges the existing system with spending the years of the young upon a branch of knowledge that few ever turn to use. It then lays out the plan of the school: a day-school for the neighbourhood, with a graded series of classes, the period of instruction divided by the clock into short parcels, the mutual instruction of the pupils, and the government of the house by a code of detailed rules for the teacher, the assistant, and the registrar. The curriculum, the largest part of the book, enumerates the useful branches: the mother tongue, the modern and ancient languages, the mathematical and physical knowledge, the logic and analysis of the human mind, the moral and political branches, the arts and employments, and the matter of taste, each with its subdivisions and its relative value. The argument throughout is economic as well as pedagogic, measuring the cost of instruction against the quantity of use produced, and treating the classical monopoly as a job in the market of education.
narrative_structure: A single treatise in numbered parts: the statement and defence of the chrestomathic name and plan, the details of the school and of its management, and the enumeration of the branches of useful knowledge with their several precepts.
literary_form: educational treatise and institutional plan; didactic prose with a curriculum scheme
meter_and_prosody: Technical, enumerating, expository prose of the jurist applied to the schoolroom: coined terms, numbered divisions, and an relentless arithmetic of time and utility, with occasional dry sallies against the established system.
historical_context: Published in the year of the controversy over the monitorial schools and of the quarrel between the rival national systems of education, and designed to be embodied in a school actually opened in London a few years later on the day principle. Its utilitarian measurement of knowledge belongs to the same school of legislative reform that in the same years was remapping the law, the prison, and the poor-law.
literary_significance: It is one of the founding documents of the secular and utilitarian critique of classical education, anticipating the long nineteenth-century argument for scientific and modern education and for the day-school, and it supplied the analytical vocabulary of curriculum and of school management. Its influence on the educational writings of the reforming school, and on the later debate over the value of the classics, was considerable, though the school it planned was short-lived.
attribution_notes: Attribution uncontested; the work is securely documented among the undisputed writings of its author, whose manuscripts and correspondence record the long delay between the plan's conception and its printing.
bibliographical_notes: First published London, 1816, in the author's own name, under a long descriptive title announcing it as a collection of papers explanatory of the design of a school of useful and scientific knowledge; a second edition followed, the school it projected was opened in London a few years later, and the text is included in the collected editions of the works.

title: The Rationale of Reward
alternative_titles: Rationale of Reward
description: The complement to the writer's penal theory, and the first systematic attempt to make a science of the rewards a legislator holds out rather than the punishments he inflicts. It was issued in English from a French editor's recension of the manuscripts, and it examines emolument, bounty, pension, prize, patent, honour, and salary as instruments measured by the happiness they purchase.
plot_or_argument: The rationale begins by classifying the masses of reward, the pecuniary and the honorary, the subsistence and the emolument, the prime and the collateral, and by stating the general rule that the quantity of reward is to be judged by the quantity of service it obtains at the least cost to the public. It then examines the modes of holding out encouragement: competition and contract, which it prefers as the cheapest instruments, against monopoly, premium, and bounty, which it exposes as purchase of the same service at a doubled price and as the nursery of sinister interest. The application to official station is the sharpest part of the book: salaries are to be adequate, transparent, and proportional, pensions are to be the reward of extraordinary service and not the patronage of the court, and hereditary honour is tried by its utility and found wanting. The closing discussion treats the reward of talent in literature and in the arts, the patent law as an encouragement of invention, and the moral sanctions, good-reputation and the sympathies, as a currency the legislator must employ but must not corrupt.
narrative_structure: A treatise in chapters of classification and application, running from the definition and division of rewards through the several institutions of emolument to the honorary and moral sanctions, in the analytic order of the author's manuscripts.
literary_form: treatise of legislation and political economy; analytical rationale of institutions
meter_and_prosody: Analytic, taxonomic, unsparing prose: subdivision after subdivision, the coined nomenclature, the interrogating aside, and an relentless reduction of reverence to account.
historical_context: Published in the years of the debates on official economy, placemen and pensions, and the reform of the civil list, and after the penal code discussion of the preceding decade, to which it stands as the other half of one theory of sanctions. The English issue followed a French recension of the author's manuscripts, and it reached the reforming public just as the review journals were making utilitarian doctrine a party question.
literary_significance: It is the classical utilitarian treatise on incentives, and one of the earliest attempts to analyse the whole system of public rewards as an economic instrument, a programme that anticipates the later economics of incentives and the administrative argument for salaried, accountable office. Its attack on monopoly, bounty, and hereditary honour supplied the reforming generation with some of its standard arguments, and its nomenclature entered the vocabulary of the science of legislation.
attribution_notes: The substance is securely the author's, but the English text is at second hand, made from the manuscripts through a French editor's arrangement, so that the order and the phrasing of the printed book belong partly to the editor's recension rather than to the author's own final shaping.
bibliographical_notes: First published in English London, 1825, in two volumes, from the author's manuscripts in the hands of a French editor; it was reprinted in the collected edition of the works, where the manuscript order was restored.

title: Rationale of Judicial Evidence
alternative_titles: The Rationale of Judicial Evidence
description: The great analytical assault on the rules of evidence as then administered, printed in five volumes at the close of the author's life from long-accumulated manuscripts. Its principle is that evidence is the arm of justice and that every rule which excludes true evidence, upon a presumption of untrustworthiness, sacrifices real justice to a fiction of law.
plot_or_argument: The work begins by defining judicial evidence as the species of address by which the persuasion of the existence or non-existence of a fact is produced in the mind of the judge, and by distinguishing the substantial from the adjective, or the course of procedure by which it is conveyed. It then attacks the exclusionary system: the rules that shut out the testimony of interest, of parties, of convicts, of the unbelieving and of children, are shown to be at once illogical, since interest does not always corrupt veracity, and mischievous, since their operation is to defeat the just cause and to enrich the profession by the delay they cause. The positive part analyses the several classes of evidence, direct and circumstantial, real and personal, original and transmitted, with their several degrees of probative force, and it examines the arts of trustworthiness, the sanctions of oath and of punishment, and the securities of publicity, of oral examination, and of the free minutes of the judge. The closing argument is constitutional as well as forensic: that a system of evidence built for the benefit of the judges and of the fee-fund is incompatible with the greatest happiness of the community, and that the substitute must be the simple method of a natural procedure before a single judge with full publicity.
narrative_structure: Five volumes in numbered books and chapters: the definition and division of evidence, the exhibition of the exclusionary rules with their exposed absurdities, the analysis of the several kinds and their probative tendencies, the securities for trustworthiness, and the plan of a non-exclusionary procedure.
literary_form: legal and analytical treatise; jurisprudence of evidence with procedural reform
meter_and_prosody: Pitiless, voluminous, satirical analysis: the endless subdivision, the reductio ad absurdum carried on for pages, the inventories of absurdity, and a comic indignation that treats the law as a system of organised delusion.
historical_context: Printed in the year of the author's death and of the beginning of the great procedural reforms, out of manuscripts composed over decades in the interval of the parliamentary and law-reform agitation, and addressed to a public already trained by the review journals to expect a utilitarian criticism of the institutions of the common law. Its matter had appeared in part through a foreign recension before the English original was published.
