literary_significance: It is one of the founders of the analytic study of evidence and of procedure, the book which first subjected the exclusionary rules to a systematic test of their consequences, and an ancestor of the nineteenth-century reform of pleading, of the witness rules, and of the modern law of evidence. As a style it is the extreme example of the legislative analytical manner, and its exposure of the 'fictions' and fee-interests of the law stands among the most sustained pieces of argumentative invective of the period.
attribution_notes: The substance is securely the author's; the printed arrangement was made from his manuscripts by another hand, and the relation between the English recension and the earlier foreign edition leaves the order of the published volumes partly an editorial construction.
bibliographical_notes: First published London, 1827, in five volumes, prepared from the author's manuscripts; reprinted in the collected edition of the works, where the materials are arranged differently, and again in a single-volume abridgement of the following generation.

title: The History of British India
alternative_titles: History of British India
description: A three-volume history of India written wholly out of books by a clerk of the governing company, and the most influential and most offensive English history of the subcontinent for a century. It divides Indian history into three civilisations, the Hindu, the Muslim, and the British, and it argues that the Hindu period was one of stationary ignorance and despotism out of which only European science and law could carry the country.
plot_or_argument: The first volumes survey the Hindu state of society: the religion, the mythology, the literature, the sciences, the laws, and the institutions of caste, of all of which the historian judges that they exhibit a people sunk in the lowest depth of intellectual and moral degradation, governed by a priesthood and by a military aristocracy, without accurate knowledge, without useful art, and without a sense of human dignity. It then traces the Muslim conquests and dynasties, whose tyranny and turbulence it holds to have changed nothing essential, and passes to the entrance and progress of the European companies, the wars and policy by which the British power was made paramount, and the administration of the provinces. Throughout, the test applied to every institution is that of utility: whatever promotes knowledge, security, and the interests of the many is approved, and whatever rests upon superstition, upon hereditary rank, or upon the caprice of a ruler is condemned. The closing argument pleads for a government of laws and of education, and for the substitution of a directed administration for the patronage and the commercial interest which had hitherto governed the territories.
narrative_structure: Three volumes: the first two on the Hindu and Mahometan civilisations, arranged by subject as religion, arts, sciences, and institutions; the third on the British progress and administration, arranged as a narrative of events with the closing analysis of the company's affairs.
literary_form: philosophical and national history; utilitarian history of civilisation with administrative argument
meter_and_prosody: Bare, dogmatic, generalising prose, contemptuous of ornament and of the picturesque, with the sweeping judgement and the summarising catalogue; the style of a reasoner who measures everything against a single standard.
historical_context: Written over more than a decade of leisure hours by a writer of the radical school while the territories of the governing company were administered under the patronage system, and published just before its author took an official charge of the company's education and appointments, from which he was long able to act upon the principles of the book. It supplied the historical teaching of the company's college and of the administration for generations.
literary_significance: It is the classic example of the philosophic history written in the study without travel, and the book on which the British governing class in India was educated; its periodisation of Indian history into three epochs and its denial of a civilisation to the Hindu period became the orthodoxy of the administration and, in the following century, the thesis which Indian writers undertook to refute. Its authority and its arrogance together make it one of the most significant and most criticised works of the intellectual history of empire.
attribution_notes: Attribution uncontested; the share of the author's son in the later editions, and of several specialist writers in the notes on the law and sciences of the country, are recorded in the history of the editions, and the book is properly cited by edition.
bibliographical_notes: First published London, 1817, in three volumes; second and third editions were prepared in the author's lifetime, and the later editions, with the appendixes and notes of the author's son, held the field into the middle of the century, when the abridgements for the schools and for the college made the text standard.

title: Elements of Political Economy
description: The compactest textbook of the Ricardian school, written to make the science of wealth teachable and to settle the controversies of the day by a few rigorous definitions. It states the doctrine of value, of wages, of profit, and of rent in the shortest and hardest form, and it argues that political economy is not the art of making a nation rich but the exposition of the laws according to which wealth is produced and divided.
plot_or_argument: The elements first define wealth as the things useful and agreeable which are the objects of desire and the subjects of production, and political economy as the science of those phases of human conduct which arise from wealth; they then distinguish productive from unproductive labour, and show that the produce of a country is made up of rent, profits, and wages, divided among the three classes of proprietors, capitalists, and labourers. The doctrine of value is settled by labour, and the celebrated argument on demand proves that demand is not the creator of production but only the rule by which the quantities of the several commodities are adjusted to the wishes of the consumers, so that the notion that public or charitable expenditure can enrich a nation by stimulating demand is exposed as a fallacy. Wages are determined by the proportion of population to capital, profits by the cost of maintaining labour and by the fertility of the marginal land, and rent is the excess of the produce of the better lands, which rises with the progress of population and falls with its relief from foreign supply. The closing chapters apply these principles to the corn laws, to taxes, to colonies, and to the currency, and argue that every device for the protection of one class at the cost of the whole is a mistake in science as well as an injustice.
narrative_structure: A short treatise in numbered sections, opening with the definitions and divisions of the science, proceeding through production, value, wages, profit, and rent, and closing with the applications to legislation, in the order of a syllabus for the lecture room and the examining board.
literary_form: treatise of political economy; textbook of the abstract method
meter_and_prosody: Taut, catechising, axiomatic prose, without illustration or apology: definition, proposition, and consequence, with a plain contempt for the fallacies of popular reasoning.
historical_context: Published in the year of the Ricardian ascendancy and of the quarrel over the corn bill, in a cheap series designed to carry the science to the educated general reader, and written by a man whose history of the empire had just established his official reputation. Its most quoted doctrine, that demand does not regulate production, was aimed at the current arguments for public spending and for the protection of agriculture.
literary_significance: It became the standard elementary text of the classical political economy, the book by which a generation was first taught the science, and the source of the 'elements' style of exposition which the abstract method made dominant. Its wages-fund doctrine, its treatment of value by labour, and its argument against the demand fallacy remained points of controversy for the hundred years of the science.
attribution_notes: Attribution uncontested; the later editions, one of which received notes and an appendix from the author's son, are the ground of the only bibliographical question, which concerns the edition and not the writing.
bibliographical_notes: First published London, 1821, as a volume of a cheap companion series; a second edition with additions appeared in the following decade, and the text was repeatedly reprinted, abridged, and translated, the annotated edition of the middle of the century becoming the common version.

title: Vindiciae Gallicae
alternative_titles: Vindiciae Gallicae: A Defence of the French Revolution and its English Admirers
A Defence of the French Revolution
description: The most learned and most generous of the replies to the counter-Revolutionary constitutional argument, written in a few months of furious work by a young Scottish lawyer and published in the spring of 1791. It accepts the issue of abstract right which the counter-Revolutionary book had refused, and answers the historical pleading with a philosophy of rights, of progress, and of the perfectibility of institutions.
plot_or_argument: The defence begins by denying that the age of a constitution is an argument for its excellence, and by asserting the right of every generation to choose its own government; prescription, it urges, is the sophistry of interest, and the true lesson of history is that institutions resting on force and on superstition must be expected to fall. It then examines the state of France before the Revolution, and argues that the burthens of the people, the privileges of the few, and the anarchy of the law made some great change not an evil but a duty; the horrors of the contest are met with the parallel horrors of every successful reformation, and the argument from the licence of a people newly freed is answered by the mischief of a people never trusted. The constitution of the following year is then defended as a settled and temperate scheme of representative government, and the English admirers of the Revolution are vindicated from the charge of disaffection. The closing pages turn upon the influence of the new principles upon the future improvement of the world, and the whole is animated by the belief that the Revolution is the beginning of a moral and intellectual emancipation of the species.
narrative_structure: A single continuous argument in numbered sections, opening with the statement of the two rival theories of the state, proceeding through the history and condition of the old government, the criticism of the objections, and the defence of the new constitution, and closing on the prospects of the species.
literary_form: political pamphlet and philosophical vindication; argumentative defence in sections
meter_and_prosody: Diffusive, earnest, learned prose of the philosophical jurist: the long period, the historical illustration, the sympathetic abstraction, and a moral fervour which its author afterwards qualified.
historical_context: Composed rapidly in London in the winter of 1790-91 at the instance of a publisher who wanted an immediate answer to the constitutional writings of the season, and published in the year in which the first French constitution was completed and the party rupture opened in England. Its author, a physician's son of Glasgow who had taken a Scottish medical degree and turned to law and to letters, wrote as a friend of the American and French principles alike, and the book made his name at once.
literary_significance: It is the ablest philosophical defence of the Revolution in English, and the text which the counter-Revolutionary argument most feared; it supplied the radical tradition with its answer to prescription, and its argument on the right of innovation, on representation, and on the education of a people to freedom passed into the reform literature of the next century. Its author's own later reservations, and the pamphlet's fate as the credential of a career that ended on the bench and in the service of the state, make it one of the most quoted cases of the change of opinion in a revolutionary generation.
attribution_notes: Attribution uncontested; the work is securely documented among the undisputed writings of its author, whose later qualifications of its doctrines are recorded in his own correspondence and in the biographical memoir of his son.
bibliographical_notes: First published London, 1791, as a separate pamphlet; it reached a second edition in the same year, was reprinted more than once before the close of the century, and was reissued posthumously with the memoir and papers of the following generation.

title: The Edinburgh Review
alternative_titles: The Edinburgh Review, or Critical Journal
description: The quarterly journal which made the critical review into a literary and political institution, founded in 1802 by a small group of young Whigs and long identified with the criticism of the age. Its unsigned articles reviewed books as occasions for argument on constitution, finance, education, and taste, and its method, at once liberal in opinion and severe in judgement, gave the review its modern authority and its modern weapons.
plot_or_argument: The enterprise of the journal was to carry into the criticism of books the analytical method of the moral and political sciences, and to treat every considerable publication as evidence upon some question of principle; accordingly its numbers interleave the review of a poem, a history, or a treatise of law with a discussion of the condition of the country, of the administration of the colonies, of the currency, or of the laws for the poor. Its declared rules forbade personal and party invective in form, while its practice made the exposure of an opponent's principles its most relished performance; and its attacks upon the poets and novelists of the day, upon what it took for the egotism of one school and the dullness of another, became the most discussed literary quarrels of the period. In politics it trained a generation to liberal Whiggism, argued for the reform of the criminal law and of representation, and by its treatment of Ireland, of the slave trade, and of the colonies made the review a branch of public business. Its later history, the long editorship, the rejection of contributions for want of space, and the rival quarterlies it provoked, belong to the social no less than to the literary history of the century.
narrative_structure: A continuously issued quarterly of reviews and state papers, each number several hundred pages of independent unsigned articles, with the occasional list of new works at the end; the unit is the article and the series is the work.
literary_form: critical review and periodical essay; the unsigned journal as a collective work
meter_and_prosody: The manner of the school of the review: lucid, argumentative, and caustic, passing from the summary of the book to the principle it raises, with the dry parenthesis, the mock concession, and the sententious close; the prose of a tribunal rather than of a chat.
historical_context: Founded at Edinburgh in 1802 by four friends, of whom the first two editors were its two most conspicuous critics, printed in Edinburgh and published in London, and sustained at first against the handicaps of a Scotch and Whig undertaking in a loyal and Tory reading public. Its earliest numbers coincided with the war, with the suspension of the habeas corpus, and with the quarrel over the new poetry, and its prosperity made every party found a journal.
literary_significance: It is the founding institution of the modern critical review, the model which the rival quarterlies and the century's magazines copied, and the tribunal before which the literature and the policy of a generation were tried. Its influence upon the practice of the essay, upon the relations of author and public, and upon the diffusion of the liberal creed is larger than that of any single book of the period; and the controversy it raised about the power of criticism over letters is one of the permanent subjects of the literature of the age.
attribution_notes: The articles were published without the writer's signature, and the attribution of individual numbers to individual hands rests on correspondence, manuscript, and internal evidence and is still revised by the editors of the collected articles; the two founders who served as its editors are recorded here as the authors of the undertaking.
bibliographical_notes: First number issued October 1802, printed at Edinburgh and published in London at eight shillings and sixpence the quarter; the series ran continuously through the century, and the early numbers were reprinted in collected editions with indexes and with tables of the contributors.

title: Elements of Chemical Philosophy
description: The first attempt of the new chemistry to state itself as a complete philosophy, made out of the matter of its author's lectures by its most brilliant expositor; only the first part of the projected treatise appeared. It gathers the doctrines of the elements, of the atomic theory, and of electro-chemical affinity into a systematic account of the science, and it closes with the most quoted prospectus of the power of chemical discovery over the arts of life.
plot_or_argument: The work begins with a statement of the objects and methods of chemical inquiry, of the distinction between the elements and the compounds, and of the evidence by which a substance is proved simple or compound, and it then enumerates the simple bodies known to the science with their sensible and measured characters. It proceeds to the doctrine of combination: the laws of definite proportions and the theory of the atoms, the nature of chemical affinity, and the order of the compounds, are stated as a system in which the philosophy of the science is separated from its technique. The middle divisions handle the chemistry of the gases, of the acids and the bases, of the metallic earths and alkalis, and of the saline and organic bodies, in a sequence of classes and of their mutual relations. The largest and most original part is the electro-chemical doctrine: that the attractions of chemistry are of the same nature as the electricity of the machine and of the great battery, that combination is a case of the union of the opposite electricities, and that the decomposition of the fixed alkalis and of the earths by the battery is the proof. The treatise ends with the application of the science to the arts, to manufactures, and to agriculture, and with the confident peroration that the day will come when the forces of nature shall be called to the service of man.
narrative_structure: A single large volume in numbered sections: the objects and elements of the science, the laws of combination and the atomic theory, the classification of the compounds, the electro-chemical theory, and the applications; the projected second part never appeared.
literary_form: scientific treatise; systematic philosophy of chemistry with experimental evidence
meter_and_prosody: Elevated and imaginative scientific prose, technical precision joined to a rhetoric of power, attraction, and life; the lecture manner of the greatest talker of the schools, with its enthusiasm kept within the definition.
historical_context: Published in the year of its author's knighthood and at the height of his chemical work, out of the discoveries of the preceding decade, the decomposition of the fixed alkalis and of the earths, the arguments on the hydrochloric and hydrofluoric acids, and the great battery of the metropolitan institution; it belongs to the moment when the revolution in chemical nomenclature and the electrical researches of the author's own school had made a new statement of the whole science possible.
literary_significance: It is the founding systematic text of the new chemistry in English, the book by which the electro-chemical dualism and the atomic doctrine were set before the British student, and a landmark in the literature of science as rhetoric: its closing passage on the command of the forces of nature became one of the most quoted sentences of the industrial age. Its influence on chemical teaching and on the practical chemists of the following decades is recorded in its many editions and translations, and its pages remain the best document of the imaginative habit of the science at the moment of its greatest expansion.
attribution_notes: Attribution uncontested; the volume is the first only of the treatise its author planned, and the matter of the unfinished second part appears in his separate papers and in the posthumous collections of his scientific writing.
bibliographical_notes: First published London, 1812, by J. Johnson, in one volume with plates; the projected second part did not appear, and the work was reprinted with the author's other scientific writing in the collected edition of his works.

title: Researches, Chemical and Philosophical
alternative_titles: Researches, Chemical and Philosophical; Chiefly Concerning Nitrous Oxide, or Gaseous Oxide of Nitrogen
description: The early volume of experiments which made its author's reputation, gathered from the work of a Bristol institution founded for the medical use of the new air, and chiefly concerning the gaseous oxide of nitrogen. It records the inhalations made upon the author's own body and upon his friends, the history of the compound and of its elements, and the observations on respiration and on animal heat which were the beginning of his chemical philosophy.
plot_or_argument: The researches first state the composition and the properties of nitrous oxide, the proportions of its elements and the proofs of its nature, and then give an account of the machine and the method by which the gas was prepared and administered at the institution. The largest part is the record of the inhalations: the sensations produced, the elevation of the imagination, the vivid pleasure, the loss of the sense of time and of place, and the different effects upon different constitutions, all set down with a frankness of self-observation unusual in scientific writing. From these the author draws the practical inference that the power of the gas over sensation may be turned to the relief of pain, and the note that it may perhaps be used with advantage in surgical operations is the most quoted sentence in the book. The closing papers extend the inquiry to respiration, to the source of animal heat, and to the union of the gases with oxygen, and they state the general doctrine, afterwards to be the frame of his chemistry, that the changes of bodies are the result of the attractions of their parts and of the electrical powers of their elements.
narrative_structure: A single volume of separate papers and memorandum-records: the chemical history of the gas, the series of inhalations with their reported sensations, the concluding medical and physiological observations, and the appendix of the experimental details.
literary_form: experimental reports and scientific treatise; medical and chemical writing with self-observation
meter_and_prosody: A curious mixture of the technical memorandum and the lyrical report of sensation: plain experimental prose interrupted by passages of rapturous self-analysis, in the language of the philosophy of feeling as well as of the laboratory.
historical_context: Issued at Bristol from the Pneumatic Institution founded by a physician for the trial of the new gases in disease, and written during the years when the author, a young apprentice to the trade, was making the experiments that carried him to the metropolitan lectureship. Its subject lay on the border of chemistry, medicine, and the psychology of sensation, and its publication fixed the reputation of the school of the new air.
literary_significance: It is at once a founding document of electro-chemistry and of the physiology of respiration, and one of the most remarkable books of the age for its frank registration of altered consciousness; the suggestion of anaesthesia in its pages became one of the great unfinished chapters of medical history, and its accounts of the visions and the elevated feeling of the gas have made it a standing document in the history of the romantic interest in the alternations of the mind.
attribution_notes: Attribution uncontested; the records of the inhalations were partly kept with the help of the institution's assistants, and the clinical cases reported were in part those of other practitioners, as the volume itself states.
bibliographical_notes: First published Bristol, 1800, by Biggs and Cottle, for the institution, in one octavo volume; it reached an enlarged second edition in the following year and was translated at once, and its papers were afterwards reprinted with the author's other early chemical work.

title: An Inquiry into the Causes and Effects of the Variolae Vaccinae
alternative_titles: An Inquiry into the Causes and Effects of the Variolae Vaccinae, Known by the Name of the Cow Pox
description: The short pamphlet which founded vaccination, published at its author's own expense and containing the evidence for a proposition drawn from the observation of the dairy counties: that the cow pox, a disease of the udder of the cow transferred to the hand of the milker, confers upon the human being an immunity from the small pox which nothing else does. It is a model of the patient accumulative method, twenty-three cases stated, compared, and argued.
plot_or_argument: The inquiry begins with the history of the opinion in the western counties, that a person who has taken the cow pox from the hand of a milking woman cannot afterward be infected by the small pox, and with the examination of the several circumstances of the disease in the cow and in the human subject. It then reports the cases in order: the progress of the inoculated cow pox from the pustule to the areola and the scab, its mild constitutional effect, and its unlikeness to every other pustular disease; and after the series of cases it records the decisive experiment, the insertion of the matter of the small pox into subjects who had previously taken the cow pox, with the finding that no disease followed. The causes of the irregular and failing cases are then examined, the identity of the matter and of the disease in the several instances is discussed, and the differences between the cow pox and the greedy itches of the horse are distinguished. The argument closes with the practical inference that an inoculation so safe may be made universal, and with the proposal of the procedure to the profession and to the public.
narrative_structure: A single pamphlet of some seventy pages in three movements: the historical and medical statement of the disease, the series of twenty-three reported cases with the experimental proofs, and the general remarks on the causes, the irregularities, and the practice.
literary_form: medical and scientific writing; case-based experimental inquiry and practical proposal
meter_and_prosody: Modest, deliberate, evidential prose of the country practitioner: the case stated in order of date with the particulars of the subject and of the pustules, the careful qualification, and the unhurried generalisation from the accumulated instances.
historical_context: Published in the year when the inoculation of the small pox, long practised and long disputed, was at once fashionable and distrusted, when the cattle trade of a grazing county carried a disease of the udder into the hands of the dairy people, and when an English physician of Gloucestershire, trained in the metropolitan schools and a correspondent of the great experimenters of the day, was able to test a country tradition by the method of the hospital. Its reception ranged from instant adoption to the warmest professional ridicule.
literary_significance: It is one of the few short books which changed the practice of medicine and the destiny of populations, the founding text of immunology and of the public vaccination which in the following century abolished the worst of the endemic scourges of the world; and as a document of method it is a classic of the argument from accumulated cases, often cited for the combination of country observation, experiment, and caution with which a national prejudice was turned into a universal practice.
attribution_notes: Attribution uncontested; the priority of the observation and the several shares of the country practitioners and of the metropolitan institutions in the trials are matters of a well-documented contemporary controversy which concerns the honour of the discovery rather than the authorship of the pamphlet.
bibliographical_notes: First published London, 1798, printed for the author and sold by the bookseller who issued it, in one thin octavo with the plates of the pustules; a second edition with the further cases appeared within the year, and translations followed immediately.

title: The Life of Lorenzo de Medici
alternative_titles: The Life of Lorenzo de' Medici, Called Lorenzo the Magnificent
description: The first considerable English history of the Italian Renaissance, built as a life of the Florentine ruler and prefaced by an introductory view of the history of Italy before his age. It rests upon manuscript matter gathered in Italy as well as upon the printed authorities, and it made its author's European reputation with the companion life which followed.
plot_or_argument: The introductory view traces the rise of the communes, the divisions of the guelfs and ghibellines, and the fortune of the house of Medici to the position from which Lorenzo governed; the life then follows his policy, the maintenance of the balance of the Italian states, the league made against the conspiracy of the Pazzi, and the journey to Naples by which, at the height of a crisis, he shifted the fortune of the war by his personal presence and his address. Alongside the narrative runs the history of the revival of letters and of the arts: the Platonist circle, the poetry and the architecture, the collectors and the schools, and the magnificent patronage with which the prince of a republic made Florence the court of Europe. The moral judgement is severe as well as admiring: the genius, the taste, and the political dexterity are allowed their praise, but the corruption of a free constitution under the forms of it, the spending of the public money upon private splendour, and the cultivation of luxury as an instrument of power are handled as the ruin of the country; the book closes with the death of Lorenzo and with the view of the French invasion and of the anarchy that followed his burial.
narrative_structure: Two parts: the introductory view of Italian history before the age of the Medici, and the life itself in continuous narrative with the historical and literary disquisitions and the notes of the authorities bound in; the whole closes with the fortunes of the immediate successors.
principal_characters: Lorenzo de' Medici; Giuliano de' Medici; the conspirators of the Pazzi; the scholars and artists of the Florentine circle; the princes and statesmen of Italy
literary_form: prose biography and historical narrative; the life with an introductory survey and scholarly annotation
meter_and_prosody: Dignified, circumstantial, moralising narrative prose of the Whig historical school, with the full period, the balanced judgement of character, and a constant consciousness of the example to modern times.
historical_context: The work of a country-bred lawyer and banker of the great trading community who had retired from practice to letters, made out of years of reading and out of manuscript copies obtained in Italy, and published in the decade in which the French invasion of Italy and the controversy over the French Revolution gave the fall of Italian liberties a direct political bearing. Its author sat afterward for the town of his residence in the short Parliament of the abolition era, and was the centre of a circle of learning and of the arts in the port.
literary_significance: It fixed for English readers the image of the Renaissance and of its most famous patron, and it established the historical method of the English liberal treatment of Italy, the authority against which the later students, from the historians of the age to the travellers of the nineteenth century, measured their own judgments. Its political moral, that a cultivated despotism disguised as a republic destroys the liberty which makes culture possible, was one of the most influential readings of Italian history of the revolutionary decade.
attribution_notes: Attribution uncontested; the book's reliance upon the manuscript transcripts obtained from Italian libraries and upon the counsel of an antiquary friend is stated in the work itself and in the correspondence of the author's family.
bibliographical_notes: First published London, 1796, in volumes with the introductory view and the notes; new editions, enlarged and accompanied by the papers of the family, appeared in the following decade, and the work was translated into Italian.

title: The Life and Pontificate of Leo the Tenth
alternative_titles: The Life and Pontificate of Leo X
description: The companion and sequel of the life of the Florentine ruler, a history of the papal pontificate at the moment when the revival of letters and the Reformation met. It rests upon manuscript evidence gathered in the Italian and Roman libraries, and it made its author's reputation as an accurate scholar of the age of the Medici popes.
plot_or_argument: The work opens with the election of the second Medici pope, with the expectations of the cardinals and of the court, and with the pomp of the beginning of the pontificate, when the genius of the age was spent upon the buildings, the festivals, and the patronage of Rome. It then follows the affairs of the state of Europe through the leagues, the wars, and the diplomacy of the Italian powers, and the government of the church through the councils, the dispensations, and the exactions by which the revenue of the court of Rome was sustained. The largest part is the history of the beginning of the Reformation: the indulgence traffic, the appearance and the progress of the great heresiarch of Saxony, the diplomacy of the papal agents, the bull and the burning of the decree, and the interviews and the disputation by which the breach was made incurable, all judged from the side of a liberal Protestant historian who holds the corruption of the court responsible for the loss of the unity of Christendom. The closing volumes survey the literature and the art of the pontificate, the fortunes of the house of Medici, and the death of the pope amid the ruin of Italian affairs.
narrative_structure: Several volumes in continuous annalistic narrative, with the books of the controversy and of the state of Europe divided among the occasions of the pontificate, and with the disquisitions upon the learning and the arts of the age bound into the history.
principal_characters: Leo the Tenth; the cardinals and courtiers of the Roman pontificate; the reformers and the agents of the indulgence traffic; the princes of Europe and of Italy
literary_form: prose biography and pontifical history; historical narrative with disquisitions and scholarly annotation
meter_and_prosody: Massed, circumstantial, judicial narrative prose: the long period of the balanced character, the accumulated evidence, and a Protestant moderation which keeps its severity within the courtesy of the scholar.
historical_context: Published in the year of the author's other historical labours and of the closing of the wars of the revolutionary age, out of the same mass of transcripts gathered in Italy as the former life, and addressed to a British public for which the Reformation, the papacy, and the fate of Italian liberty were live questions. Its author was by then the chief ornament of the learned circle of the great port and a member of the short Parliament of the abolition era.
literary_significance: It long held the field as the English history of the pontificate which opened the Reformation, and its combination of recovered manuscript evidence with a liberal judgement of the papal court made it a standard authority and an offence to the Roman censor; the two lives together founded the English historical study of the Renaissance. Its reading of the Reformation as the moral consequence of the corruption of the court, and of the age of Leo as the brilliant and corrupt union of letters and priestcraft, remained a presence in the historical imagination of the following century.
attribution_notes: Attribution uncontested; the volume of the manuscript materials obtained from the Italian libraries, and the share of the family papers in the later editions got up by the author's son, are recorded in the biographical and bibliographical accounts.
bibliographical_notes: First published London, 1805, in several volumes; new editions appeared in the following decade, with the replies to the strictures of the Roman censure and with the additions of the later editors, and a family edition with the memoir followed after the author's death.

title: The Wrongs of Africa
alternative_titles: The Wrongs of Africa, a Poem. Part the First
description: The first of the great abolition poems, written at the request of the committee of the cause and published in two parts, the first in 1787 and the second in the following year. Its subject is the whole progress of the trade, from the coast of Africa through the voyage to the colonies, and its method is the plea of humanity made in the heroic line against the interest of a nation.
plot_or_argument: The first part opens upon Africa in its peace and its innocence, the domestic affections and the simple life of its people, and passes to the arrival of the trading ships and to the arts by which the victims are caught: the treachery of the traffic, the wars raised to procure captives, and the seizure of the husband, the parent, and the child. It then sets before the reader the prison, the march to the shore, and the embarkation, and urges upon Britain the argument from her own love of liberty, from the Christian name, and from the plain justice of the case, that a trade carried on by such means is a national crime for which the country must answer. The second part pursues the subject to the other side of the ocean, the voyage and the treatment in the colonies, and closes with the argument that the abolition is the duty as well as the interest of a trading people, and that the true commerce of Africa is in her freedom and in the produce of cultivated labour.
narrative_structure: A poem in two parts, each in books of descriptive and invective sequence: the picture of Africa, the seizure and the march, the plea to Britain, then the voyage and the colonies, with the closing argument and the appeal to the conscience of the nation.
principal_characters: The people of Africa; the captured husband and father; the slave trader and his crew; the planter and the colonists; the people of Britain addressed as the judges of the cause
literary_form: abolitionist verse in the descriptive-complaint manner; poem of argument and appeal
meter_and_prosody: Blank verse of the heroic line, sustained by apostrophe and invective, with the pathetic domestic picture and the direct national address usual to the poetry of the abolition cause.
historical_context: Composed for the movement opened by the committee of the friends of the abolition, in the year of the first petition to Parliament and of the great pamphlet warfare of the trade's defence, and issued by the publisher of the cause with a preface by a friend of the author. Its author, a banker and scholar of the greatest slave-trading port in the kingdom, stood by the trade's victims against the interest of his own town and of his own family.
literary_significance: It is the founding poem of the abolitionist agitation and one of the most influential of the poems which forced the slave trade into the literature of the period; it fixed the humanitarian pictorial sequence, the innocent Africa, the treacherous seizure, the broken family, and the appeal to national conscience, which the oratory, the prints, and the novels of the next forty years repeated. Its history is also a chapter in the social history of literature: a trade poem written against the commerce of its author's own community, and welcomed by the committee as the voice of the cause.
attribution_notes: Attribution uncontested; the two parts were published in successive years and the poem was completed no farther, and the prefatory matter of the first part is from another hand than the poet's own.
bibliographical_notes: Part the first published London, 1787, by R. Faulder, in a thin octavo; part the second followed in 1788, with an American impression in the same year, and the two parts were reprinted together in the collected editions of the author's poems.

title: The Butterfly's Ball, and the Grasshopper's Feast
alternative_titles: The Butterfly's Ball
description: The most enduring of the poems written for children of the period, a gay assembly of the insects of the garden given as an entertainment for the young, and printed in the smallest of the little volumes which the nursery trade made its own. It is at once a party piece, a natural-history lesson, and a miniature masquerade, and it passed into the nursery language of two continents.
plot_or_argument: The poem invites the company of insects to the ball of the butterfly and the feast of the grasshopper, and musters the guest list of the garden and the hedge, the beetle, the fly, the moth, the bee, and the rest, with their several graces and their several follies. It then describes the company in assembly, the music, the dance, the supper, and the merriment, till the hour and the accident break up the party, and the little readers are left with the joke and the lesson of a pleasure that is over. The charm of the piece is its complete seriousness about a fantastic scene, the manners of a ball-room applied to the creatures of the summer grass, and the courtesy with which the smallest insect is introduced and remembered.
narrative_structure: A single short poem of invitation, muster, entertainment, and breaking-up, in continuous rhymed verse with the list of the company as its central movement.
principal_characters: The butterfly; the grasshopper; the company of the garden insects, the beetle, the moth, the fly, and the bee
literary_form: children's poem of the beast-fable and assembly manner; the nursery party piece
meter_and_prosody: Brisk rhyming couplets of comic nursery verse, with a triple-time swing and the refrains and catch-phrases of the children's song; the measure of the piece is one of the reasons of its memory.
historical_context: Written by a man of letters who was also the historian of the Medici and the abolition poet, and first printed in the small volume of the nursery trade of the years after the turn of the century, when the picture-book and the gift-book for very young children became a distinct branch of publishing; it was reprinted with cuts through the century and crossed to America at once.
literary_significance: It is one of the two or three poems which every generation of English-speaking children has said before it could read, and a landmark in the history of the verse written for the nursery, since with it the assembly of the creatures of the garden became a stock of the children's book. Its influence on the later animal-party poem, and its permanence as a piece of popular recitation, are among the curiouser facts of literary history, and its author is remembered by it rather than by his histories.
attribution_notes: Attribution uncontested; the poem was long circulated also in a prose version and with the added moral of the later nursery editors, and the earliest issues are small and imperfectly recorded.
bibliographical_notes: First published 1807, in a small duodecimal volume; it reached an issue of the following year with engravings, and countless British and American reprints, often with the plates of the toy-books and with the added precept of the editors of the middle of the century.

title: Original Poems for Infant Minds
alternative_titles: Original Poems, for Infant Minds, by Several Young Persons
description: The first successful collection of verse written for very young children as children, issued in two volumes in 1804 and 1805, and made by two sisters with the contributions of other hands. It set the pattern of the nursery lyric: the short poem of the common object, the animal, and the duty, put into the mouth of the child and meant to be repeated by him.
plot_or_argument: The collection is a series of short lyrics, dialogues, and little narratives for the infant reader, arranged without a general argument but with a definite moral intention: the lesson of kindness to animals, of duty to parents and to the poor, of truthfulness, of the observation of the works of nature, and of the gratitude owed to the giver of all. Its poems teach by the concrete instance, the sheep, the dog, the bird's nest, the sick neighbour, the little reader's own hour and his own play, and they carry the child through a graduated range of feeling from the mere naming of the thing to the reflection upon death, upon duty, and upon the Creator. Alongside the moral pieces run the poems of simple observation and of the fancy, the description of the seasons and of the trades of the country, which give the collection its hold upon the notice of the child rather than upon his fears.
narrative_structure: Two volumes of independent short poems, graded in difficulty and length for the reading and recitation of very young children, with the preface and the advertisements of the publishers of the juvenile line; the units are single lyrics and dialogue-poems.
principal_characters: The infant speaker and the children of the several little narratives; the animals and the common objects about the nursery and the village
literary_form: juvenile verse of the nursery lyric and the moral lesson-poem
meter_and_prosody: The simple stanzas of infant recitation: common measure and short lyric lines, hymn-like quatrains, and the dialogue in the smallest possible compass, with the reiterated moral close.
historical_context: Issued from the juvenile trade of the metropolis in the years when the educational market for children's books was newly formed, out of the commission of a publisher who wanted verse of a class and a price for the very young, and read in the families and in the Sunday and day schools of the century that followed. The chief hands in the collection were two unmarried sisters of a dissenting family, one of them afterwards a known writer and painter, the other the more famous verse-maker of the pair.
literary_significance: It is the beginning of the English nursery lyric proper, and the book from which the poem of the common object and the small moral duty took its form; it trained several generations of children in their first recitations, and its manner, at once simple, didactic, and observant, is the source of the popular verse which has since been repeated to and by very young children.
attribution_notes: The collection is a joint venture published under a collective designation, and contains matter by several hands besides the two sisters who wrote most of it; the distribution of the individual poems between the several contributors is settled by the memoranda and by the later family editions, and the sisters are the authors recorded here.
bibliographical_notes: First published in two volumes, London, 1804 and 1805, in the juvenile series of the house of the publisher; the volumes were reprinted and abridged throughout the century, with the family editions and with the illustrated issues of the American press.

title: Rhymes for the Nursery
description: The successor of the infant poems, and the source of the most sung poem in the English-speaking nursery. It carries the verse for very young children a step further into the sheer fancy and the song, and it contains the little lyric of the wondering child before the distant light which became, set to an older air, the universal rhyme of childhood.
plot_or_argument: The volume is a collection of short rhymes and songs for the nursery, of three kinds: the lyric of wonder and of the fancy, the little narrative of the child and the animal, and the rhyming lesson of the duty and the consequence. Its most famous poem addresses the distant twinkling light with the child's naked question, and passes from the wonder of the thing seen to the comparison of the small lamp of the evening and to the closing reverence of the maker; the pieces about it run through the sports, the pets, the seasons, and the small morals of the nursery day, in the smallest possible measure and with the emphasis always upon the sound and the repetition. The intention throughout is to give the child verse he can learn by ear, and to make the learning of the first words a pleasure rather than a task.
narrative_structure: A single volume of independent short rhymes, without argument or sequence of subjects, arranged in no order of matter but in the order of the reciter's pleasure and command of the words.
principal_characters: The wondering child; the little creatures and companions of the nursery rhymes; the objects of the evening and of the garden
literary_form: juvenile verse of the nursery rhyme and song
meter_and_prosody: Short rhymed couplets and stanzas of the song measure, in the trochaic and iambic swing of the rhyme meant to be sung or chanted; the emphasis on the sound, the reduplication, and the easy close.
historical_context: Published in the year following the second volume of the infant poems, from the same juvenile trade and by the same two hands, in the season when the picture-book and the song-book for the very young child became a staple of the nursery and of the Sunday school. One of its lyrics was set almost at once to the continental air which has carried it round the world, and it has been translated into a great number of languages.
literary_significance: It holds the single poem which is known, in some language or another, by more children than any other verse in the world, and it fixed the form of the nursery lyric of wonder, in which the child's question about the sky is asked without explanation; its little rhymes have been the first verse repeated by generation after generation of children, and its place in the history of the reading of the young is quite out of proportion to its size.
attribution_notes: The volume is the joint work of the two sisters, the greater number of the pieces being by the younger, whose lyrics have since been separated from her sister's by the family editors and by the history of the juvenile trade; the individual attribution of several rhymes has been variously reported in the reprints.
bibliographical_notes: First published London, 1806, in a small volume of the juvenile series; reprinted and imprinted constantly through the century, in the British and the American nursery editions, with the airs and with the coloured plates of the later toy-books.

title: The History of Little Henry and his Bearer
alternative_titles: Little Henry and his Bearer
description: The little Indian tale which made its author's fame and which was read as a children's book for three quarters of a century: the story of an English child left in the hands of a native servant in the company's territories, and of the knowledge of the Bible which passed from the child to the man. It is a founding text of the missionary story for children and of the English picture of domestic life in India.
plot_or_argument: The history opens with the little English child placed under the care of his bearer in an Indian station, where the family's own round is broken and the child is left almost wholly with the native servant; and it tells how the child's simple reading of the Bible, his cheerfulness, and his talk about the Saviour, wrought upon the mind of the attendant, who in his turn becomes a student of the scriptures and a secret teacher of his own countrymen. The narrative follows the separations of the child's life, the trials and the sickness of the servant left behind, and the steadfastness of a faith which had been taught without art; the closing pages report the death of the bearer and the account of his hope, and pass into the argument that the religion which had reached one Indian heart by the means of one English child may be trusted for the conversion of the whole country.
narrative_structure: A single short tale in continuous sequence, framed by the letter and the report of the narrator, with the closing argument upon the field of India added as the moral of the story.
principal_characters: Little Henry; his bearer; the household and the servants of the Indian station; the narrator and the family at home
literary_form: juvenile and devotional tale; the domestic narrative with a missionary argument
meter_and_prosody: Plain, tender, earnest narrative prose, with the direct little speech of the child and the elevated close of the devotional appeal; the style of the tract-tale at its most winning.
historical_context: Written by a young officer's wife resident in the company's territories, out of the domestic life of the stations and of the evangelical interest in the missions of the war years, and printed first in India and afterward in the metropolis, where it was put out by the religious book-sellers and carried to every nursery. Its subject lay upon the two great public interests of the moment, the missions and the education of the children of the settlement.
literary_significance: It is the most influential of the children's tales of the missionary movement, and the book by which generations of English readers first conceived the religious claim upon India; its picture of the child as the teacher and of the servant as the convert supplied the stock pattern of the missionary story, while its representation of the native and of the station has made it, in the modern history of writing about empire, one of the most studied and most criticised of children's books.
attribution_notes: Attribution uncontested; the tale was long reprinted in abridged and in combined issues, sometimes with the sequel and sometimes with the other Indian tales of the same pen, and the first Indian and English impressions are distinguished in the bibliography of the author's works.
bibliographical_notes: First published in 1814, an impression being printed in India and the metropolis issue following from the religious book-sellers; it was continuously reprinted for seventy years in the juvenile and Sunday-school series, with the sequel and with the collected little books of the author.

title: The History of the Fairchild Family
alternative_titles: The Fairchild Family
description: The most famous and the most feared of the English books for children of the nineteenth century, a history of three children and of the religious discipline of their home, published in parts beginning in 1818 and long read in every family of the middle rank. It puts before the child the whole course of a pious day, the duty, the fault, the punishment, and the forgiveness, and it carries its lesson to the verge of the terrible.
plot_or_argument: The history sets the Fairchild children in their house in the woods, with their father and mother as the governors of a little commonwealth of which the rule is the Bible and the catechism, and it follows their lessons, their work, their play, and their sins. Its central method is the severe object-lesson: the children are taken to the remains of the body of an executed criminal, that they may see what the wages of guilt come to; they are punished with a public severity which the modern reader finds hard, and they are taught to read, to give to the poor, to visit the cottages, and to consider their own hearts. The narrative passes through the illness and the death of one of the children, the trial of the survivors, the gipsy and the beggar episodes, and the steady government of the parents, whose religion is at once tenderness and terror. Later parts carry the family forward to the growth and the trials of the survivors, and the whole book is a manual of the discipline of the soul applied to the very young.
narrative_structure: A continuous family history in numbered chapters, published in parts and in volumes, each part a sequence of the occasions of the home, the lesson, the fault, and the consequence, with the hymns and the readings bound into the narrative.
principal_characters: Mr and Mrs Fairchild; Lucy, Emily, and Henry Fairchild; the poor, the gipsy people, and the dependents of the neighbourhood; the survivors of the family in the later parts
literary_form: juvenile and domestic tale; the religious family history for home instruction
meter_and_prosody: Plain, urgent, unembellished narrative prose of the devotional teacher, with the direct speech of children, the solemn parental address, and the inserted hymn and scripture; its effect rests on the plainness of the moral said.
historical_context: Published from 1818 by the book-seller of the religious and the fashionable trade, in the season of the evangelical family and of the tract for the young, when the religious instruction of children at home was a serious concern of the middling ranks and when the theory of the child's depravity was taught as frankly as the theory of his innocence. Its author, an officer's wife returned from India, had already written the little Indian tale, and the Fairchild books were followed by the third part and by imitations without number.
literary_significance: It is the type and ancestor of the English religious family book for children, and one of the few children's books that has become a subject of cultural history in itself: its mixture of piety, fear, and the terrible object-lesson has been read ever since as the image of a whole method of governing the young, and its influence on the children's literature of both countries, and upon the nineteenth-century conscience about education, is very great.
attribution_notes: Attribution to a single pen is uncontested; the book is nevertheless a long series rather than a fixed text, since the later parts were given out at a great interval after the first, and the many abridgements, the edited and the expurgated issues of the later century alter the text materially, so that the work is cited by part and by edition.
bibliographical_notes: First published London, 1818, by the book-seller of the religious and the fashionable trade, in parts and in a volume; the later parts were given out at long intervals, the series closing in the late 1840s, and the several parts appear with varying dates in the catalogues, which should be consulted when the part is cited. The whole was reprinted, abridged, and revised through the century in Britain and America, and the cheap and the Sunday-school issues differ materially from the first.

title: The Little Woodman and his Dog Cæsar
alternative_titles: The Little Woodman and his Dog Caesar
The History of the Little Woodman and his Dog Cæsar
description: A tale for children, first published in 1818 and reprinted without end through the century, of the youngest child of a poor woodman's family, of the cruelty of his elder brothers, and of the fidelity of the dog Cæsar; one of the most widely read of the English books of the exposed child and of the brute that serves the innocent.
plot_or_argument: The tale opens in the hut of a woodman of the forest country, whose family is poor, whose elder sons are hard and envious, and whose youngest, the little William, is a child of gentleness and of the book. Upon the father's death the burden of the household falls upon the brothers, and the wickedness of the elder sons, prompted by the greed of the portion and by hatred of the piety of the little boy, carries him into the forest and leaves him there to perish by hunger and by the beasts. The dog Cæsar, bound to the child by the tenderness of his rearing, watches over him in the woods, defends him against the wolf that stalks him, and becomes the means of the discovery of the guilt; the cruelty is searched out, the guilty brothers come to ruin, and the preserved child is provided for and brought forward in his little education. The argument of the book is the religious argument of the whole class of these tales: that Providence keeps the innocent, that the sin of the household is found out in its own time, and that the reading of the Bible and the duty of gentleness to the young and to the brute are the whole wisdom of the child.
narrative_structure: A single continuous tale for the young reader, in short chapters of the plain domestic narrative, moving from the hut and the forest to the exposure, the preservation, the discovery, and the religious close, with the direct address of the moral to the child at the turn of the several parts.
principal_characters: The woodman and his wife; the little William, the youngest of the family; the elder brothers, hard, idle, and envious; the faithful dog Cæsar; the neighbours and the people of the forest country who search out the crime
literary_form: juvenile and devotional tale; the domestic narrative of the injured child with the animal fidelity
meter_and_prosody: Plain, urgent, and affecting prose of the evangelical teacher for the young reader, with the little speech of the child, the terror of the forest scene told in short unadorned sentences, and the solemn tenderness of the moral; the pathos of the brute's fidelity is gained by the restraint of the style.
historical_context: Published in 1818, the year which gave the world also the religious family history of the same pen, in the season of the cheap and the Sunday-school book, when the tale of the persecuted child and of the faithful animal was the most powerful instrument of the juvenile trade and when the terror and the tenderness of such stories were held necessary to the formation of the conscience of the labouring and middling ranks. Its author, an officer's wife long resident in the company's territories, had already written the Indian child's tale, and the woodman's story became, with her other little books, a standing possession of the nursery and of the circulating juvenile libraries of both countries.
literary_significance: The type of the evangelical tale of the exposed child and of the ministering animal, and one of the most permanently remembered of the books of the English nursery: the figure of the faithful dog and the scene of the forest are among the stock images of juvenile writing, and the tale has been read ever since as the exemplar of the method by which terror, pathos, and providential justice were combined for the moral use of children.
attribution_notes: Attribution uncontested; the title is variously given at length and at abbreviature in the later issues, the name of the dog and the spelling of the title being altered in the reprints, and the tale was also issued in the combined juvenile volumes and in the abridged cheap series, which do not follow the first text.
bibliographical_notes: First published in 1818; the early cheap and religious reprints follow, among them the issue of the later religious house of F. Houlston and Son, catalogued at about 1825, and the small picture editions of the closing century. The tale was reprinted constantly in Britain and in America in the juvenile and Sunday-school series, and the first edition should be consulted where the text is quoted.

title: Practical Education
alternative_titles: Practical Education, Inferred from the Principles of Philosophy
description: The great English treatise of educational practice of the turn of the century, written in two volumes by two hands of one household, a father and his daughter, and profounded in the title to be inferred from the principles of philosophy. It carries the science of the mind from the lecture-room into the nursery and the schoolroom, and it reports, in the plainest of all such books, the experiments of a large and cultivated family upon the powers of children.
plot_or_argument: The work reasons from the principles of human nature, as they had been settled by the philosophy of the preceding century and by the modern enquiry into the powers of the mind, to the practice of education, and it treats in the successive chapters of the management of the infant from the cradle, of the principles of human nature as they appear in children, of the education of the feelings and the passions, of attention, of association, of the love of distinction and of sympathy, of early prejudice and of the learning of languages, of memory and of amusement, of the studies proper to the several ages, and of the moral discipline of the young. Its governing conclusions are that the child should be governed by the natural consequences of his actions and by the desire of approbation rather than by the task, the rote, and the rod; that whatever is to be known should be learned from the thing and the experiment rather than from the description in the book; that the powers of the mind are earned by practice in the affairs that interest them; and that the greatest error of the existing method is the teaching of words instead of ideas. The illustrations are drawn for the most part from the anecdotes of the children of the household and of the pupils of the family, and the argument is everywhere carried by the reported instance.
narrative_structure: A treatise in chapters, in two consecutively paginated volumes, each chapter a separate branch of the subject built of the philosophical principle, the familiar instance from the nursery or the school, and the practical rule; no continuous narrative runs through the work, but the several chapters are bound together by the reiterated appeal to the same domestic experience.
literary_form: conduct and educational treatise; the practical philosophy of the mind applied to the nursery and the school
meter_and_prosody: Clear, brisk, familiar argumentative prose, the style of the experimenting household: the principle stated plainly, the instance told as a little story with warmth and humour, and the rule deduced without ornament. Its characteristic manner is the anecdote used as evidence, and its sentence is short, unacademic, and addressed to parents rather than to schoolmen.
historical_context: Published in 1798, the year of the treatise on population and of the strictures on the modern system of female education, in the season of the dissenting academy, of the educational projects of the philosophical radicals, and of the new attention to the infant mind which came from the philosophy of the preceding age and from the Continental book on the education of the child. The household from which the instances were drawn was itself a school of experiment, and the book was the first public product of a partnership of parent and child which continued in the juvenile stories and the letters of the following decades.
literary_significance: One of the most influential books of educational practice in the English language, and the point at which the doctrine of association of ideas was turned into a method of teaching; it changed the practice of the nursery and of the better schools of both countries for two generations, supplied the vocabulary of the education controversy of the nineteenth century, and stands at once as a document of the history of childhood, of the philosophy of mind, and of the literary work of a family, being the first published fruit of one of the most remarkable pens of the following age of fiction.
attribution_notes: The shares of the two hands of the household are not distinguishable in the first edition, which was given out without the names of the writers, and the division of the volumes between them has been variously guessed by the editors and the biographers, the daughter's hand being claimed for the more of the illustrative matter and the father's for the metaphysical statement, without decisive evidence. The work is therefore entered as collaborative, and the several chapters have been attributed now to the one and now to the other writer.
bibliographical_notes: First published London, 1798, in two consecutively paginated volumes, by the bookseller and publisher of the philosophical and reforming list; a second edition followed in 1801, and the work was reissued as essays, separately and collected, in the writings of the two hands, and in the later school and family editions. The text of the first edition is that properly cited, the later issues being revised and partly re-cast by the writers themselves.

title: An Experiment in Education, Made at the Male Asylum of Madras
alternative_titles: An Experiment in Education, Made at the Male Asylum of Madras; Suggesting a System by which a School or Family may teach itself, under the Superintendence of the Master
description: The founding document of the monitorial system of education, a brief report by the medical officer of the asylum of the Company's settlement at Madras of the experiment by which the fatherless children kept there were taught by one another, and by which a school might, in his phrase, teach itself under the superintendence of the master.
plot_or_argument: The report states the condition of the male asylum at Madras, the insufficiency of its funds, the idleness and ignorance of the boys, and the failure of the common method of teaching them by the master alone; and it then describes the device by which the difficulty was overcome: the most advanced of the scholars were made the instructors of the rest under him, the school being divided into classes, the boys examined and promoted, the meritorious marked and rewarded by badges and by the honour of the station, the monitors responsible for the proficiency of their several classes, and the master retaining only the general superintendence and the religious instruction. He sets out the progress made, the smallness of the expense at which the boys were thus taught, and the certificates of the officers and of the directors who had seen the school; and he argues that the same machinery, applied in England to the children of the labouring poor, would give a national education at a price within the reach of a parish or a subscription. The whole method rests, in his statement, upon the emulation of the boys and upon the economy of the pupil-teacher.
narrative_structure: A short report of an experiment, in the manner of the statement of facts: the case of the asylum, the method pursued, the proof of the progress made, the account of the expense, the appended letters and certificates, and the closing proposal of the system's extension.
literary_form: educational report and treatise; the institutional experiment with the evidence and the plan of extension
meter_and_prosody: The blunt, particular, unadorned prose of the practical man stating a case, with the enumeration of the classes, the marks, and the rewards, the figures of the expense, and the appeal to the testimony of persons of authority who had visited the school; the style is that of the official memorandum rather than of the essay, and its force lies in its air of evidence.
historical_context: Written out of the eleven years' residence of the author's experiment at Madras, where he had taken the asylum in hand in the years after the American war, and published in London in 1797, in the season of the charity and Sunday school, of the societies for the education of the poor, and of the first anxiety about the instruction of the manufacturing and labouring classes. The notice it obtained among the directors, among the friends of the missions, and at length in the highest families, prepared the way for the great monitorial controversy of the following twenty years, in which the same method was promulgated in England by another schoolmaster with the public credit of the metropolis.
literary_significance: The originating text of the monitorial or mutual system of instruction, and one of the few short pamphlets of its age whose machinery was copied into the schoolrooms of three continents; the arrangement of pupil-monitors, classes, badges, and registers which it described became the working form of the elementary schools of the established religious society and of its rival, and so of the mass schooling of the nineteenth century, which makes it a central document of the history of education and of the education of the poor.
attribution_notes: Attribution to a single hand is uncontested; but the dating of the several tracts and the priority of the invention were the subject of a long and bitter dispute with the other promulgator of the same method, in which the parties pleaded the Madras experiment of the 1780s and the Southwark school of the 1790s against each other, and the controversy must be consulted wherever the claim to the invention is in question.
bibliographical_notes: First published London, 1797, printed for Cadell and Davies in the Strand, a thin pamphlet with the letters and certificates appended; a second edition and the enlarged statements of the system followed, together with the accounts of the schools established upon it, and the tract was reprinted in the collections of the writings of the promoters of mutual education.

title: Improvements in Education, as it Respects the Industrious Classes of the Community
alternative_titles: Improvements in Education
description: The published account of the school at Southwark by its Quaker founder, the book which brought the monitorial method before the public of the metropolis and made the mutual system a party, a subscription, and in time a national institution; a report of an experiment like the Madras statement, but written for the town and its subscribers rather than for the Company's settlement.
plot_or_argument: The work describes the school of the author's opening in Southwark, in which a great number of children of the labouring classes were taught by one another under his single superintendence at an expense of a few shillings for each child in the year, and it sets out the machinery by which this was done: the classes, the monitors, the patrol of the yard, the slate, the sand, the wall for the first lessons, the marks of merit and of demerit, the register of the progress, the rewards of the badge and the public inspection, the arrangement of the hour of study, and the moral and religious teaching delivered to all without the doctrine of any party. It argues that the poor may thus be taught numerously, cheerfully, and at a price which makes the education of the industrious classes a subject for the subscription of the public, and it urges the political uses of the method, the obedience, the cleanliness, the habit, and the knowledge which it gives being the securities of the order of the country. The several parts are supported by the account of the expenses, the examination of the visitors, and the evidence of the masters of other schools.
narrative_structure: A report in the manner of the second edition of the educational statement: the account of the school, the description of the method in its order of proceeding, the evidence of the proficiency made, the estimate of the expense, the replies to the objections, and the appeal to the public, with the papers of the inspecting society and the certificates appended.
literary_form: educational report and treatise; the school statement with the plan for the education of the labouring classes
meter_and_prosody: Plain, businesslike, persuasive prose of the schoolmaster addressing his subscribers, with the minute enumeration of the arrangements, the repetition of the figures of cost and numbers, and the frank appeal to the feelings of the reader for the children of the poor; less technical and more hortatory than the Indian statement of the same method.
historical_context: Published in 1803, after five years of the school at Southwark which he had opened for the children of the labouring poor under the inspection of a friendly society of subscribers, in the season of the anxiety about the discipline of the manufacturing population, of the Sunday-school movement, and of the project of a national education; the book won the subscriptions and the visits of the great, including at length the countenance of the court, and it set forward the rival claim of priority to the Indian system which the same method had already obtained, the two parties dividing the public and the religious aid of the following generation.
literary_significance: With the Madras statement of 1797 it is the foundation text of the monitorial system, and through the British and Foreign School Society, the free schools, and the model normal schools of the nineteenth century its machinery became the working form of popular education in Britain, America, and the colonies; its claim to teach the children of the poor cheaply, in numbers, and without sectarian doctrine is one of the governing ideas of English social reform, and the book itself is a primary document of the history of the elementary school.
attribution_notes: Attribution to a single hand is uncontested; the title is variously abridged in the many editions, and the enlarged later issues, given out in parts and with the memoir of the author prefixed, contain matter not in the first; the long priority controversy with the promulgator of the Indian system obliges the careful citation of the edition.
bibliographical_notes: First published London, 1803, printed for the author and sold by the booksellers of the religious and the philanthropic trade, with the subtitle advertising the account of the school at Southwark and the application of the Indian method; it went through many editions and into several European translations, a second part and the several abridgements for the schools following, and the later issues were prefixed with the life of the author and the reports of the society which grew out of his work.

title: A New View of Society
alternative_titles: A New View of Society; or, Essays on the Principle of the Formation of the Human Character
description: The founding book of English Socialism, four essays published anonymously by the manager of the greatest cotton works in the kingdom, laying down the principle that the character of every human being is formed for and not by him, and arguing from that doctrine that the vices and the misery of the labouring population are the necessary product of their early training and circumstances, and may be changed with them.
plot_or_argument: The first essay states the principle of the formation of character: that every individual, from the cradle, is made such as he is by the circumstances which have surrounded him, by the opinions that have been placed before him, and by the training he has received, none of which he could control; so that selfishness, crime, and misery are to be pitied and remedied rather than punished, and no man is properly the author either of his own vices or of his own merit.
