The following essays apply the doctrine in order to the established religion and the divisions of the churches, to the existing arrangements of private property and of the relations of the sexes, and to the practice of government, arguing that the institutions of the country, the punishments of the law, and the rival sects of religion are themselves products of the old system of formation and must give way when the conditions of the people are changed. The practical proof is drawn from the management of the manufacturing population under the writer's own care, where the children were received into the infant school, the reading, writing, and arithmetic and the habits of cleanly and orderly life were taught without the rod, the dwellings, the shops, and the hours of the village were amended, and the general intelligence and good behaviour of the working people were thereby increased together with the profit of the concern; and the closing appeal is to the legislature and to the magistrates to provide a national education as the first measure for the cure of the distress and the demoralisation of the labouring classes.
narrative_structure: Four essays in a single argument, the first stating the principle and the rest applying it successively to religion, to the social institutions, and to practice; the plain statement of the doctrine, the illustration from the existing system, and the evidence of the experience of the works, with the appended accounts of the establishment and the letters of the visitors, the whole being enlarged by the added essays of the later editions.
literary_form: social and educational treatise; the essays on the formation of character with the report of the practical experiment
meter_and_prosody: Plain, earnest, declaratory prose of the practical projector, with the long affirmative period, the perpetual appeal to fact and to twenty years' experience, and the serene confidence of a writer who reasons as if his whole question were settled by the stating of it; the style carries conviction by its air of benevolence and command rather than by wit or subtlety.
historical_context: Written in the years of the writer's management of the Lanarkshire cotton works, when the machinery of the manufacturing system, the distress of the labouring classes after the peace, the infant-school movement, and the projects of the education societies were all before the public, and published in 1813 anonymously, the copies being sent to statesmen, to philosophers, and to the princes of the blood, and the work being announced to a London dinner of the friends of the reform. It belongs to the harvest of the doctrine of circumstances which came from the French writers of the eighteenth century and from the English associationist psychology, and it was the immediate provocation of the long literature of the communities and of the co-operative schools of the following two decades.
literary_significance: The central text of the English literature of education, of character, and of social regeneration, and the book from which the co-operative movement, the writers of the communities, and much of the later reforming writing of the century took their doctrine that circumstances make the man and that the circumstances may be made; its influence ran through the factory reform, the school-boards, the co-operative movement, and the American communities of the 1840s, and as a document of the self-made reformer's faith in his own principle it holds a first place in the prose of argument of the period.
attribution_notes: Published anonymously, the copies being given out without the writer's name, and the later editions and the collected issues of the writings carry the authorship openly; the essays were enlarged and re-stated in the several editions, and the appended practical accounts vary between the issues, so that the text is best cited from the edition with the writer's own annotations.
bibliographical_notes: First published London, 1813, in four essays, for the writer and the booksellers of the philosophical and reforming list, the several editions being enlarged by the writer himself; a collected edition with the reports and the letters followed in 1817, American reprints appeared early, and the essays were reissued in the selections of the writer's works and in the modern scholarly editions, which note the several additions.

title: A Report to the County of Lanark
alternative_titles: A Report to the County of Lanark; of a Plan for Relieving Public Distress and Removing Discontent, by Giving Permanent Productive Employment to the Great Mass of Skill Labour
Report to the County of Lanark
description: The most concrete and the most radical of the great plans of social regeneration of its age, drawn up as a paper for the meeting of the freeholders and householders of the county of Lanark and given to the public as a report of the managers of the manufacturing village: a proposal for home colonies of agriculture and manufacture which should employ the ruined labour of the country and educate the people into a new character.
plot_or_argument: The report begins with the experience of twenty years' management of a manufacturing population, and with the demonstration that the habits, the health, the intelligence, and the productiveness of the same people may be raised together by a changed arrangement of their schooling, their dwellings, and their labour. It then states the cause of the public distress of the years after the peace: that the productive power of the country, increased infinitely by machinery and by skill, has produced far more than the consumers who are paid wages can consume, so that the plenty of the country and the poverty of its makers exist together, and the labourer is unemployed because he cannot be paid in the old way. From this he argues, not for relief by gifts, but for a permanent plan: the establishment throughout the kingdom of villages or home colonies of from five hundred to two thousand persons, upon grounds of a thousand to two thousand acres, each colony laid out with the dwellings, the schools, the kitchens, the workshops, and the gardens in one square of good building, the agriculture and the manufactures joined in the same body, the children educated at the common cost from the earliest years, and all the labour lightened by machinery and by combination. The expense he computes, and proposes to meet it from the parochial and county funds and from the poor-rate already raised, the colonies being managed by committee of the persons interested; and he pleads that the plan saves the country, the law, and the morals of the people at once, and removes both the distress and the discontent of which the county meeting had sat.
narrative_structure: A report and address in the form of the county paper: the statement of the experience, the analysis of the causes of the distress, the plan of the home colony in its detail of numbers, ground, building, and education, the estimate of the expense and of the returns, and the closing appeal to the county and to the legislature, with the resolutions of the meeting and the several letters appended.
literary_form: social report and project; political economy of public distress with the plan of the home colony
meter_and_prosody: The flat, fluent, statistic prose of the manager addressing his county, with the long periodic sentence, the confident enumeration of numbers, acres, and pounds, and the perpetual appeal to the experience of twenty years; a style of proposal which persuades by the weight of its particulars and by its benevolence rather than by analysis or wit.
historical_context: Drawn up after the meeting of the freeholders and inhabitants of the county of Lanark at Hamilton in the closing months of 1820, in the depth of the distress of the manufacturing and agricultural labourers which followed the bad harvests, the returning officer's accounts of the poor-rates, the pressure of the restrictive and corn laws, and the agitation of the great meeting of the metropolis for reform; and it belongs to the decade of the plans, the county meetings, and the parliamentary inquiry which made the condition of the labouring population the first question of the day.
literary_significance: The chief document of the proposal for regeneration by the village of united and mutual co-operation, and one of the most influential of English plans of social building: the home colony described in it governed the co-operative and the community writing of the 1820s and 1830s, was pleaded before the poor-law commissioners and the boards of health of the following generation, and anticipated the modern literature of the model village, the garden city, and the planned community; its analysis of distress as the product of excessive productive power joined to deficient means of consumption is one of the notable economic arguments of its time.
attribution_notes: Attribution to a single hand is uncontested; the report is given out in the name of the managers of the establishment in the first issue, and the writer's own authorship is stated in the collected editions; the several reprints of the plan, the letters to the counties, and the reports of the co-operative bodies restate the proposal with alterations of detail.
bibliographical_notes: Published as a report of the managers of the village establishment at New Lanark to the county of Lanark, at Glasgow and in London, in the closing months of 1820 and in 1821, the year of the first edition being entered variously in the catalogues as 1820 and as 1821 since the paper was prepared for the meeting of December 1820 and given out to the public in the following year; it was reprinted in the collected editions of the writer's works and separately in the co-operative press, and the plan was restated in the later letters and reports.

title: The Principles of Political Economy
alternative_titles: The Principles of Political Economy: with a Sketch of the Rise and Progress of the Science
description: The manual which made the doctrine of the English school of political economy a textbook, a compact and heavily instanced exposition of the science in its newest form, prefixed with a sketch of the rise and progress of the study, and set out with the plain assertion of the abstract method against the popular writers on wealth and the practical errors of the day.
plot_or_argument: The work states the principles of the science in the order of wealth, treating of production and of distribution, and holding that value is regulated by the quantity of the labour required in production, wages and profit being determined by the cost of production and the competition of capital, and rent by the difference of the powers of the soil, and not, as the common doctrine held, as a deduction from the returns of the farmer. It argues at large against the errors of the writers on the commercial policy, against the notion that the accumulation of stock and the application of machinery injure the labourer on the whole, against the paradoxes of under-consumption and of the distrust of plenty, and against the confusion of the wealth of the state with the riches of the individuals who compose it; and it treats of taxation, of the public debt, of the restrictions upon trade, and of the statistical evidence of the progress of nations. The historical sketch prefixed gives the rise of the science from the older writers, and is used as an argument that the truth of the modern doctrine is established and that its opponents are the survivors of a mistaken literature.
narrative_structure: A treatise in books and chapters, the historical sketch of the rise and progress of the science prefixed to the systematic statement of the principles, the argument proceeding from value and production to rent, profit, wages, and capital, and thence to taxation, commercial restriction, and the measure of national wealth; the several positions carried by the citation of the authorities of the science and by the numerical instance.
literary_form: treatise of political economy; the scientific exposition with the history of the science
meter_and_prosody: Clear, dogmatic, heavily instanced prose of the didactic economist, with the blunt disquisition upon the mistakes of the popular writers, the perpetual quotation and rejection of authorities, and the confident verdict upon the facts; its force rests upon the range of reading and the decision of the assertion rather than upon subtlety of method, and its sentences are built to be quoted and to settle a dispute.
historical_context: Published in 1825, Edinburgh and London, in the season in which the doctrines of the science had been settled by the chief English writer of the preceding fifteen years, in which the extra-mural classes of the Scottish metropolis were making political economy a branch of the ordinary education of the professional and commercial young, and in which the controversy on the corn laws, the currency, and the distress of the agriculture and manufactures was carried on in the review journals; its author, the writer of the standard English manual of the commerce and of the literature of the science, and at length the first holder of the chair of the subject at the metropolitan university of the reformers and afterwards the professor at Glasgow, here reduced the newest doctrine to the form in which it could be taught and contested.
literary_significance: For two generations the standard textbook of the science in Britain, America, and the colonies, and the medium through which the doctrine of value by labour, the theory of rent, and the abstract method became the received orthodoxy of the universities and of the commercial classes; its sketch of the history of the study was long the common introduction to the literature of the subject, and the book is a primary document of the professionalisation of political economy and of the vocabulary of the reform debates of the century.
attribution_notes: Attribution uncontested; the editions are many and the enlarged later issues, given out in two volumes with the added essays on taxation and on the literature of the science, differ materially from the first, and the American and the European reprints, with the translations, are variously altered, so that the citation should note the edition.
bibliographical_notes: First published Edinburgh, 1825, for William and Charles Tait, and Longman and Co, London, in one volume octavo; several enlarged editions followed, the later issues being given out in two volumes with the supplementary treatises, and the work was reprinted in the selections of the standard writers of the science, in the American editions, and in the European translations.
